ai-industry-vocabulary-2025: summary four terms defined how ai insiders talked about the technology in 2025 — "reasoning" multistep problem solving models like openai's o1/o3 and deepseek's r1 , "evals" automated safety testing before model release , "synthetic data" ai generated training data from one model to another , and "vibes" qualitative, intuition based chatbot judgment . each term reflects a specific shift in how frontier ai models were being built, tested, and evaluated that year. highlights "reasoning" refers to a model's ability to work through multistep problems, backtracking and revising as needed, rather than producing an answer in one pass — openai's o1 and o3 models and deepseek's r1 the model that "shook up silicon valley" in january 2025 exemplify this category, taking a minute or longer to answer a question but showing their intermediate steps and handling more complex problems as a result. reasoning models cost substantially more to operate than earlier ai models because of the additional computing power required per query, and whether that added capability translates into genuine economic value remains, in the words of ai researcher melanie mitchell, "still an open question." "evals" evaluations are batteries of automated tests — such as probing whether a model can be prompted into hacking a computer network or providing bioweapon synthesis instructions — that determine whether a frontier ai model is safe to release; the practice remains entirely voluntary, run by ai companies themselves alongside third party labs and government bodies like the uk's ai safety institute, with no binding requirement that a company disclose or act on unfavorable results. "synthetic data" — training data generated by one ai model the "teacher" for another the "student" — has become necessary because most advanced models have already consumed essentially all freely available human generated text on the internet; deepseek used synthetic data from one of its own models to train another, and openai separately investigated whether deepseek had also queried openai's models to generate training data in violation of openai's terms of service. synthetic data carries a specific risk: because large language models can hallucinate, an inaccurate "teacher" model produces training data that makes the "student" model dumber rather than smarter, requiring careful human monitoring of the outputs used for training. "vibes" or a "vibe check" refers to judging an ai chatbot's output by qualitative feel — whether responses are concise or overwrought, pandering or confrontational — rather than by quantitative benchmark scores; openai's president publicly endorsed vibe checks as "great evals" in their own right, not merely an informal supplement to formal testing. uc berkeley's chatbot arena crowdsources vibe checks at scale: users see anonymous, randomly paired responses from different ai models to the same prompt and vote on which they prefer, and the resulting rankings from more than two million votes since the project's 2023 launch are closely watched across the ai industry as an informal but influential measure of model quality. a research project called vibecheck attempts to formalize this qualitative judgment into measurable dimensions — ranking chatbots along continuums like serious versus humorous and formal versus informal — on the argument that these qualitative properties have a measurable, real impact on how people judge ai models even though they resist reduction to a single correctness metric. concept ai buzzwords you need to know now wsj, february 2025 defines four terms that captured specific, concrete shifts in how frontier ai models were being built, tested, and judged as of early 2025, moving beyond the more foundational ai/ml/deep learning vocabulary that had already stabilized by that point. "reasoning" describes models capable of working through multistep problems with backtracking and revision — the article's example is coordinating an all hands meeting by cross referencing calendars and room availability, a task humans perform with what feels like effortless common sense but that requires genuine multistep planning. openai's o1 and o3 models and deepseek's r1 exemplify this category: they take noticeably longer to respond than earlier models, in exchange for handling more complex problems and exposing their intermediate reasoning steps, at meaningfully higher computational cost per query. whether this translates into commensurate economic value remains genuinely contested — the article quotes ai researcher melanie mitchell's explicit skepticism that reasoning capability will necessarily prove economically valuable at the cost required to run it. "evals" evaluations are the ai industry's term for the automated safety testing that determines whether a frontier model is fit to release, probing for dangerous capabilities such as facilitating computer intrusion or providing instructions for synthesizing weapons. the article is careful to note the practice's current limitation: evals remain entirely voluntary, conducted by the ai companies themselves increasingly alongside third party labs and government bodies like the uk's ai safety institute, quoted describing evals as "early tripwires ahead of more advanced capabilities" , with no binding requirement that a company disclose unfavorable results or forgo releasing a model that fails them — a structural incentive problem the article flags explicitly. "synthetic data" addresses a scaling constraint: since most advanced models have already consumed essentially all freely available human generated text online, researchers increasingly train new models on data generated by an existing "teacher" model for a "student" model to learn from, a technique deepseek used in developing its own models and that openai separately investigated deepseek for potentially having used against openai's own models in violation of its terms of service. the technique carries a specific risk given llms' propensity to hallucinate: an inaccurate teacher model produces training data that makes its student model measurably worse, not better, requiring careful human oversight of synthetic training data. finally, "vibes" captures a notable shift in how ai insiders themselves judge chatbot quality: increasingly by qualitative feel is a response concise or overwrought, pandering or confrontational rather than exclusively by quantitative academic benchmarks. the article treats this as a legitimate methodological development rather than a lapse in rigor, quoting openai president greg brockman's public endorsement that "vibe checks are great evals" in their own right. uc berkeley's chatbot arena operationalizes this at scale — presenting users with anonymous, randomly paired model responses to vote between, accumulating more than two million votes since its 2023 launch into industry watched rankings — while a research project called vibecheck attempts to formalize the underlying qualitative judgment into measurable dimensions serious versus humorous, formal versus informal , arguing that these "soft and fuzzy" properties have a demonstrable, measurable impact on how people actually judge ai models even though they resist reduction to a single correctness score. related ai ml fundamentals — the foundational ai/ml/deep learning vocabulary and history this concept's more recent, frontier model specific terminology builds study of that shift in production, and a 2017 hbr framing of ml as a general purpose technology with concrete early business impact and risks. highlights ai, machine learning, and deep learning nest inside one another: ai is the broad goal of making machines perform tasks that normally require human intelligence; machine learning is the specific subfield that lets machines learn from data rather than being explicitly programmed for each task; deep learning is a further specialization of machine learning using many layered neural networks, particularly well suited to unstructured data like images and text. what is ai artificial intelligence machine learning was first defined by arthur samuel in the 1950s as "the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without explicitly being programmed" — a definition traditional programming can't satisfy for tasks like recognizing faces, where writing an explicit rule based program is either impractical or impossible even though humans do it effortlessly. machine learning, explained machine learning systems can serve three distinct functions: descriptive using data to explain what happened , predictive using data to predict what will happen , or prescriptive using data to recommend what action to take — and fall into three training subcategories: supervised learning trained on labeled data, the most common type in production use , unsupervised learning finding patterns in unlabeled data, useful for discovering unanticipated structure , and reinforcement learning trained through trial and error against a reward signal . machine learning, explained deep learning uses neural networks with many layers, each recognizing increasingly complex features of the data an early layer might detect an edge, a later layer might recognize that edges combine into a stop sign , and generally needs less human intervention and produces more accurate results on unstructured data than traditional machine learning — at the cost of requiring much more computing power. what is deep learning three developments made modern deep learning viable: geoffrey hinton's layered self training method each layer trains on the previous layer's output, allowing the network to build up from simple to complex feature recognition ; the sheer volume of digitized data now available to train on, since deep learning is fundamentally a brute force pattern detection process requiring vastly more examples than a human needs to learn the same concept; and the repurposing of gpus originally built for video game graphics for parallel neural network computation, which sped up training by orders of magnitude. deep learning will radically change the ways we interact with technology three types of neural network architecture serve different purposes: feed forward networks information flows one direction only, well suited to tasks like flagging a single transaction as fraudulent based on its own features ; convolutional neural networks or cnns modeled on the brain's visual cortex, well suited to perceptual/image tasks like medical scan diagnosis or logo detection ; and recurrent neural networks or rnns connections loop backward as well as forward, well suited to sequences like detecting fraud across an entire transaction history rather than one transaction in isolation . what is machine learning a foundation model is a deep learning model trained on transformer network architecture over vast quantities of unstructured, unlabeled data, usable out of the box for a wide range of tasks or adapted to a narrower task through fine tuning a much shorter follow up training pass on a smaller, labeled data set ; large language models are the subclass of foundation models specialized for processing and generating natural language text. what is deep learning a basic glossary of terms recurring across the ai/ml literature: algorithm rules telling a machine what to do with input data , hallucination confidently presented fabricated or inaccurate output , natural language processing/nlp machines analyzing and generating human language , neural network interconnected processing nodes loosely modeled on brain neurons , and token the sub word unit of text an llm processes and generates . artificial intelligence, explained google's 2016 overhaul of google translate is the canonical real world case study of the "three enabling developments" converging in production: engineers replaced the old phrase based statistical translation system with a neural network based one google neural machine translation trained on google's vast trove of translated text and run on custom built tensor processing units, producing a jump in translation quality so large that some observers described it as nearly closing the gap to human translators overnight. the great a.i. awakening by 2016, the same deep learning capability once confined to elite research labs was becoming accessible to nonspecialists through user friendly frameworks and pretrained models, mirroring how earlier eras of software development moved from specialist only to broadly accessible — a shift google's own jeff dean framed as urgent, telling a conference audience "if you're not using deep learning already, you should be." machine learning is no longer just for experts a 2017 hbr framing situates ml among history's general purpose technologies steam engine, electricity, internal combustion engine — each catalyzing waves of complementary innovation — and argues machine learning overcomes "polanyi's paradox" the 1964 observation that humans "know more than we can tell," historically blocking automation of tacit skills like recognizing a face by letting machines learn from labeled examples rather than requiring an explicit hand coded rule. the business of artificial intelligence concrete 2017 era business impact: jpmorgan chase's ml system for reviewing commercial loan contracts cut work that used to take loan officers 360,000 hours down to a few seconds; infinite analytics' ad placement ml system tripled advertising roi for a global consumer packaged goods company and drove a $125 million annual revenue increase for a brazilian online retailer's search and discovery process. the business of artificial intelligence machine learning introduces three specific new risks that traditional explicit rule software did not carry to the same degree: hidden bias inherited from historical training data e.g. a hiring model perpetuating past recruiters' demographic biases without any explicit biased rule being written , low "interpretability" since neural networks deal in statistical rather than literal truths, making it hard to prove a system will work in all cases, and difficulty diagnosing errors when they occur, since the underlying structure that produced a wrong answer can be too complex to unpack. the business of artificial intelligence machine learning tends to redesign work at three nested levels rather than eliminating entire jobs outright: tasks and occupations e.g. machine vision freeing radiologists to focus on critical cases and patient communication , business processes amazon redesigning fulfillment center workflow and layout around robots and optimization algorithms , and business models shifting from à la carte song sales to a personalized subscription station — with the most effective division of labor typically automating one or two steps of a ten step process rather than handing the whole process to a machine. the business of artificial intelligence concept artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning are frequently used as if interchangeable, but they nest inside one another as progressively narrower specializations. ai is the broad, decades old goal of building machines that perform tasks normally requiring human cognition — perceiving, reasoning, learning, problem solving. machine learning is the specific technique, first defined by arthur samuel in the 1950s as "the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without explicitly being programmed," that has become the dominant way most current ai is actually built: rather than a programmer writing an explicit rule for every case the traditional approach, sometimes called "software 1.0" , the system is given data and learns its own internal rules from patterns in that data. this distinction matters because there are tasks — recognizing a face, for instance — that humans perform effortlessly but that resist being reduced to a hand written explicit algorithm; machine learning solves exactly this class of problem by letting the machine essentially program itself through exposure to examples. deep learning is a further specialization within machine learning, using neural networks with many layers to process especially complex or unstructured data text, images, audio with less human intervention and often greater accuracy than traditional machine learning techniques — at the cost of requiring significantly more training data and computational power. what is ai artificial intelligence machine learning, explained machine learning systems can be categorized by what they're designed to do — descriptive explaining what already happened in the data , predictive forecasting what will happen , or prescriptive recommending what action to take — and, separately, by how they're trained. supervised learning trains a model on data that has already been labeled by humans e.g. thousands of images individually tagged "dog" or "not dog" , letting the model learn to replicate that labeling on new, unlabeled examples; it's the most common approach in production systems today. unsupervised learning gives the model unlabeled data and lets it surface patterns or groupings that weren't specified in advance, useful for discovering structure like unexpected customer segments that a human analyst wasn't explicitly looking for. reinforcement learning trains a model through trial and error against an explicit reward signal, telling the system when it made a good decision so it can learn, over repeated attempts, which actions lead to better outcomes — the approach behind training systems to play games or drive autonomously. machine learning, explained within deep learning specifically, three neural network architectures serve different purposes depending on the shape of the problem. feed forward networks move information in one direction only, from input layer to output layer, well suited to tasks that evaluate a single instance on its own merits — flagging one financial transaction as potentially fraudulent based on its own features, for example. convolutional neural networks cnns are structured to mirror the organization of the brain's visual cortex, making them particularly well suited to perceptual tasks like identifying a disease from a medical scan or detecting a company's logo in a social media post. recurrent neural networks rnns include backward looping connections, letting them weigh a sequence of inputs against each other rather than judging one input in isolation — useful for detecting fraud not just from a single transaction but from how that transaction compares against an individual's entire prior spending history, or for predicting how a sequence of text or speech is likely to continue. what is machine learning three specific developments converged to make today's deep learning boom possible, none of which existed together before roughly the last decade. first, geoffrey hinton and colleagues at the university of toronto developed a layered self training method: an early network layer learns to recognize simple features an edge, a contour from massive exposure to raw data, and once trained, feeds its output to the next layer, which learns to recognize more complex features built from the first layer's output a nose, an ear , and so on — hence the "deep" in deep learning, referring to the number of stacked layers rather than any depth of understanding. second, digitization produced the sheer volume of data deep learning needs, since — unlike a child who can learn a new concept from a handful of examples — a deep learning system is fundamentally a brute force pattern recognition process that typically needs to be shown millions of examples to reliably learn a pattern the article's example: showing a network 19 million cat pictures until statistically significant "cat" features emerge . third, researchers realized that gpus — originally built to handle the parallel visual rendering demands of video games — could be repurposed to run the millions of simultaneous connections in a neural network, compressing what had previously taken weeks of training into a single day. deep learning will radically change the ways we interact with technology google's 2016 overhaul of google translate is the field's own canonical illustration of these three developments converging in a real production system, documented in detail in the great a.i. awakening. the google brain team replaced translate's decade old phrase based statistical system — which translated text piece by piece with limited awareness of surrounding context — with google neural machine translation, a deep neural network trained end to end on google's enormous accumulated corpus of previously translated text and run on custom tensor processing units built specifically to accelerate neural network computation. the resulting jump in translation quality was large enough that some bilingual reviewers described the system's output as approaching human level competence almost overnight, a discontinuity the article frames as evidence that deep learning was shifting from a research curiosity to infrastructure capable of reinventing existing consumer products at global scale. the same historical moment saw deep learning begin moving beyond specialist research teams like google brain: transformer network architecture see transformer architecture and trained on vast quantities of unstructured, unlabeled data, which makes them usable out of the box across a wide range of tasks, or adaptable to a narrower specialized task through fine tuning — a much shorter, cheaper follow up training pass on a smaller labeled data set specific to the target task. large language models are the engine, electricity, the internal combustion engine — each of which catalyzed waves of complementary innovation across unrelated industries the internal combustion engine, for instance, eventually produce unreliable outputs regardless of how sophisticated the model itself is. cloud native architecture — open interfaces, apis, and telecom specific virtualization and softwarization technologies including network functions virtualization nfv , software defined networking sdn , and open ran — is the second prerequisite, because ai driven automation needs programmable, api accessible network functions to actually act on; without this layer, an ai system might correctly diagnose a network problem but have no standardized way to actually intervene and fix it. strategic approach for building ai native telecom networks beyond these two foundational layers, the roadmap calls for rethinking three specific infrastructure domains. compute needs gpus specifically for ai/ml workloads, deployed with a strategic split: model training — the more compute intensive, less latency sensitive workload — placed in private clouds, while inference — the latency sensitive workload that actually has to respond to live network conditions — is placed at the network edge, close to where decisions need to be acted on in real time. networking needs to be upgraded with smartnics network interface cards capable of offloading and accelerating data processing directly , high bandwidth ethernet 100gbe or 400gbe , and low latency interconnect protocols like infiniband or rdma over converged ethernet roce needs to shift to high performance flash storage with object storage capabilities, chosen specifically for its ability to scale and to operate coherently across hybrid and multicloud environments rather than being tied to a single infrastructure location. strategic approach for building ai native telecom networks alongside these physical infrastructure changes, the roadmap names two organizational prerequisites. first, operators need to build internal data literacy and ai expertise, specifically framed as necessary to manage proprietary datasets effectively — implying that infrastructure alone, without the internal capability to actually work with the resulting data and models, doesn't translate into functioning ai native operations. second, and connected to this, operators are advised to focus on developing proprietary ai: smaller, in house models purpose built for their own specific network conditions and needs, rather than depending entirely on third party general purpose ai vendors — the stated rationale is retaining control over where data is stored, how it's processed, and how models are trained, rather than ceding that control to an external vendor's infrastructure and roadmap. this includes a practical validation discipline: any vendor ai solution being considered should be tested and tuned against the operator's own real production data before being trusted in production, rather than accepted on the strength of the vendor's own performance claims — a discipline directly relevant given how often ai vendor claims fail to hold up under independent scrutiny see ai risk prediction tool failures . strategic approach for building ai native telecom networks the roadmap closes with an explicit expectation management point: putting these centralized manual risk review at that scale was infeasible. the hidden demand for ai inside your company an empirical study of physical robot adoption published in management science found the same hierarchy flattening effect the github copilot research documents for genai, via a different mechanism: robots make individual employee performance dramatically easier to measure in isolation, letting one manager effectively supervise more people — each $1 million in robot investment was associated with roughly a 5 person increase in average span of control, directly reducing the number of middle managers a robot adopting organization needs. why robots will displace managers — and create other jobs robot adoption doesn't shrink total employment — it polarizes the skill distribution: middle skilled roles machinists, welders, assembly line workers decline as robots take over their tasks, while both high skilled hiring to program, design, and manage the robots and low skilled hiring for tasks robots still can't reliably do, like amazon's human delivery van loaders rise enough to outweigh the middle skill losses in net. why robots will displace managers — and create other jobs concept organizational structures have historically formed around the constraints of the dominant technology of their era. the modern org chart originated with the new york and erie railroad in 1855, when executive daniel mccallum used the telegraph to coordinate work across a large workforce spread over a wide geographic area, producing what is considered the first organizational chart. henry ford's assembly line exploited mechanical clocks and standardized parts; agile software development, formalized in 2001, exploited new software tooling and internet based communication. each of these structures persisted for decades because they were built around genuinely fixed human limits — finite attention, the need for people to physically be present, the fact that adding capability to a project meant adding more people or making existing people work harder. reshaping the tree rebuilding organizations for ai ai breaks that constraint: for the first time, "intelligence" can be added to a project without adding headcount. this is already happening informally and largely unsanctioned — a 2023 salesforce survey found over half of employees using ai at work were doing so without organizational approval, and 64% had passed off ai assisted output as their own unaided work. this "shadow ai" use is possible because llms operate at human scale: they can read documents, draft emails, and adapt to context without requiring specialized training or bespoke software integration, so an individual with access to a capable model can simply start delegating tasks to it, independent of any top down rollout. reshaping the tree rebuilding organizations for ai redesigning a process around ai, rather than merely automating one step of an unchanged process, means treating ai as an added participant throughout the workflow. a described case study from a small educational software team illustrates this at the level of a single feature design process: ai personas were used to generate first pass simulated user feedback in place of or ahead of human testers; ai was used to synthesize scattered team feedback into a single agenda ahead of a meeting, shortening the meeting itself; and ai driven screenshot to code tooling let the team produce and iterate on working prototypes live during the meeting rather than only planning changes to be built later. in that account, a process that previously took roughly a week was reduced to one or two days. the same account anticipates a further step in which autonomous ai agents carry concepts through to deployed code with minimal human intervention, with humans shifting toward a supervisory role. reshaping the tree rebuilding organizations for ai from this, three principles are proposed for organizations trying to adapt deliberately rather than reactively. first, let teams develop and share their own methods for using ai, since ai performs more like an additional team member than an external it system, and top down mandates are likely to fit individual team contexts poorly; this requires incentives and culture that make employees comfortable experimenting and disclosing what they're doing. second, build processes for the more capable models expected in the near future, not just for what today's models can do, since organizational change itself takes time to implement. third, move quickly: if the efficiency gains observed in early ai experiments continue, organizations that delay experimentation risk falling behind rapidly, which argues for lightweight, bottom up experimentation guidelines rather than slow, centrally designed rollouts. reshaping the tree rebuilding organizations for ai empirical research on one specific role bears out the structural shift mollick describes in the abstract: how ai is redefining managerial roles reports a harvard business school study, led by manuel hoffmann, of 50,032 software developers observed from 2022 to 2024, half of whom used github copilot. the researchers tracked more than 2.4 million platform actions, sorting them into core work coding and managerial work coordination and project management , and found that copilot access shifted developers' task allocation toward core work +5% and away from project management 10% . two mechanisms drove this: developers using gen ai worked more autonomously and needed less coordination with others, and faster coding freed up time for exploration and learning. the authors argue this lets companies flatten their reporting structure — not by eliminating middle managers outright, but by reducing how many are needed and redirecting the ones who remain away from routine coordination, scheduling, and quality checking toward higher value hands on work and process improvement. the effect is uneven across skill levels: because less skilled workers are more likely to trust an ai system's guidance than their own judgment, they benefit disproportionately from gen ai's availability, which frees managers from a significant share of the burden of directly upskilling low performers. a companion interview with kpmg's head of workforce innovation, edwige sacco, corroborates this from inside a real organization: gen ai is blurring the line between middle manager and associate level work, since associates who use it to compress a five hour client discovery task into three hours are reinvesting the freed time in more strategic work once reserved for managers, while managers who remain increasingly focus on the human centric client conversations — reading between the lines, articulating a client's real problem — that gen ai still cannot handle. how ai is redefining managerial roles reinventing the organization for genai and llms mit smr, ethan mollick, april 2024 is a companion piece by the same researcher, published five months after "reshaping the tree," that reuses much of the same underlying material — the 1855 railroad org chart origin story, the wharton interactive case study, and the salesforce shadow ai survey statistics — while extending the argument in a genuinely new direction: the question of whether ai enabled organizational change tends toward worker control or worker coaching. prior algorithmic management uber's driver ratings, ups's route efficiency tracking already gave companies comprehensive, real time, and largely opaque visibility into worker behavior, a shift mit sloan's katherine kellogg and coauthors characterized as categorically different from traditional supervision. the article argues llms could supercharge this into a more totalizing form of control — an ai system that tracks, targets, evaluates, and rewards workers while also delivering feedback in a way that feels warm and personal, potentially making comprehensive surveillance more palatable without changing who is actually in charge. but the article treats this trajectory as a genuine choice rather than an inevitability: organizations that instead let ai remove the most tedious parts of a job, leaving employees with more interesting work, see workers respond positively in ways that support engagement and retention. translating this into practice requires the same shadow ai surfacing challenge "reshaping the tree" identifies, but the article is more specific about the incentive design required to solve it — not just permission to use ai openly, but concrete rewards explicitly, cash prizes, promotions, and flexible work arrangements for employees who surface substantial ai driven process improvements, on the logic that such incentives are a small price relative to the productivity gains at stake. reinventing the organization for genai and llms the hidden demand for ai inside your company hbr, april 2026 supplies the concrete, enterprise scale answer to a question both mollick pieces raise but don't resolve: what should an organization actually do once it recognizes its own shadow ai economy? using bbva, a 125,000 employee, 25 country bank, as its central case, the article argues that most corporate gen ai programs fail by treating employees' unauthorized consumer ai use as a compliance problem to be restricted rather than a demand signal to be redirected — a mistake, since a recent industry report found that although only 40% of companies had purchased official llm subscriptions, employees at more than 90% of those companies reported regular personal ai use for work regardless. bbva's response rested on three principles matching this concept's own thesis almost point for point: treat ai as an assistant rather than a replacement, give employees autonomy with clear accountability for results, and build a peer to peer network bbva's "champions" and "wizards" to spread knowledge rather than relying on top down it mandates. the bank moved fast compressing legal and gdpr review into two months and scaled through engineered scarcity rather than blanket rollout — an initial 3,000 licenses, allocated competitively and revoked from low users, made access a privilege rather than an obligation and created organic demand that grew usage to 11,000 active users within a year, over 4,800 employee built custom gpts, and reported time savings of 2 5 hours per week 3 4 hours per week among the 600 person internal audit team, which reached 99% adoption . governance stayed centralized on the dimension that mattered most — a hard rule that ai outputs could never write directly to core systems without human validation, backed by mandatory training and an automated "quality score" evaluating the guardrails of thousands of employee created gpts, since manual case by case risk review at that scale was infeasible. the article closes with five transferable lessons for other organizations: secure the environment quickly rather than studying the problem at length, make access attractive through scarcity rather than mandate, designate power users to diffuse tacit knowledge, train managers concretely rather than abstractly before asking them to sponsor change, and enforce human ownership of ai assisted work as a non negotiable structural constraint. the hidden demand for ai inside your company read together with the two mollick pieces, bbva's experience is the empirical proof of concept for "reshaping the tree"'s central claim that shadow ai use signals genuine organizational demand rather than a risk to be suppressed, and for "reinventing the organization"'s argument that surfacing that demand requires concrete incentives rather than mere permission — while adding operational detail engineered scarcity, a formalized champions/wizards network, an automated quality score neither theoretical piece specifies. why robots will displace managers — and create other jobs mit smr, june 2025 extends this concept's hierarchy flattening thesis beyond generative ai to physical robots, drawing on the authors' peer reviewed management science study of firms adopting industrial and collaborative robots in production. the mechanism differs from github copilot's — robots don't make individual employees more autonomous the way a coding copilot does — but the organizational effect converges on the same outcome. robots dramatically improve how precisely individual employee performance can be measured and compared, since a worker's productivity working alongside a consistent, transparent robot is far easier to isolate from teammates' contributions than performance in a purely human team; this lets one manager effectively supervise a larger group, with the study finding each $1 million in robot investment associated with roughly a 5 person increase in average span of control, directly reducing how many middle managers a robot adopting organization needs. critically, the effect isn't simple job destruction: middle skilled roles machinists, welders, assembly line workers decline as robots take over their tasks with greater consistency and falling cost, but companies that invest in robots hire significantly more high skilled workers to program, design, and manage the robots themselves and more low skilled workers for tasks robots still can't reliably perform, illustrated by amazon's continued reliance on human labor to load and operate delivery vans — with the combined increase in high and low skilled hiring outweighing the middle skilled losses in net employment terms. the article's closing case study, stanley black & decker's robot based tape inspection system, illustrates a role middle managers retain even as their ranks thin: robot collected inspection data revealed upstream production quality patterns that neither c suite executives nor frontline workers were positioned to see, and it took middle managers' cross functional vantage point to both discover the analytics opportunity and drive the resulting process fix — a concrete instance of the "role redefinition rather than elimination" pattern this concept's other sources describe for genai driven hierarchy flattening, here demonstrated for physical automation instead. why robots will displace managers — and create other jobs related ai strategy — the staged practice covered in more technical detail there agentic organizational redesign — a far more radical framework for the same underlying shift, arguing for rebuilding at the edge rather than transforming existing processes in place customer personalization strategy — applies the same "start with agile pods, not a reorg" principle specifically to personalization programs open questions the source's process redesign example is drawn from a single small internal team wharton interactive ; it does not address how the same redesign approach scales to larger organizations with more formal approval chains, compliance requirements, or unionized workforces. sources reshaping the tree rebuilding organizations for ai — ethan mollick on how technological shifts have historically reshaped organizational structure, and what redesigning work processes around ai looks like in practice. how ai is redefining managerial roles — hbr, 2025 07 01; harvard business school research on github ai-powered-robots-in-the-workplace: summary generative ai — large language models, large behavioral models, and agentic ai — is turning robots from rigidly scripted machines into adaptive systems that learn from demonstration and generalize across tasks. this is enabling a new wave of workplace deployment, from warehouse human robot collaboration to customer facing service robots and humanoid manufacturing workers, alongside the safety engineering and real world training data infrastructure that deployment requires. highlights robotics researchers describe their field as approaching "its chatgpt moment": until recently, robot behavior had to be explicitly programmed for each task, but new techniques let robots learn behaviors the way large language models learn language, through exposure to large volumes of demonstration data rather than hand coded rules. imitation learning — where a robot learns by mimicking successful human operated demonstrations, such as teleoperated "aloha" robotic arms folding shirts or tying shoelaces — has proven more reliable for delicate physical tasks than pure simulation, since real world physical interactions crumpling paper, gripping irregular objects are too complex to simulate perfectly. reinforcement learning, where a robot improves through trial and error against its own past performance as deepmind's ping pong playing robot arm did, progressing from beginner to high intermediate over four weeks , works well for bounded, clearly scored tasks but struggles in open ended physical environments where there's no obvious way to define incremental progress. skills learned by ai powered robots can transfer across contexts — a robot that learns to handle a fragile wine glass in a café setting carries elements of that skill over to handling vials in a clinic or delicate merchandise in a boutique — mirroring how large language models generalize across languages and tasks after being trained on one broad corpus. bmw's figure 02 humanoid robot, deployed at its spartanburg, south carolina plant, contributed to production of roughly 30,000 vehicles over an 11 month pilot by autonomously navigating the body shop, interpreting vague spoken instructions, and asking clarifying questions — a qualitative break from the scripted robotic arms auto factories have used since the 1980s. human robot collaboration in warehouses can be mapped on a 2x2 framework crossing the level of human capability required against the level of robot autonomy available, yielding four scenarios — robot in lead dhl's autonomous cargo unloading , human in lead hermès packers assisted by simple sealing robots , elementary hrc amazon style mobile fulfillment where robots transport racks to stationary human pickers , and advanced hrc ai optimized task allocation that adapts robot behavior to a specific human's fatigue and pace . no code programming and "fleet learning" let a frontline worker correct a robot's behavior directly — explaining and physically demonstrating a better approach — compressing operational improvement cycles from months previously requiring an it ticket or vendor visit to days, and spreading that correction across an entire robot fleet at once. the clearest deployment risk identified across service robot pilots is customer and employee trust, not the underlying technology: robots at tokyo's henn na hotel sometimes increased rather than reduced staff workload due to accent and noise related misunderstandings, and successful deployments consistently position robots as augmenting rather than replacing frontline employees, backed by concrete before/after metrics rather than abstract promises. because gen ai robots carry cameras, microphones, and persuasive conversational ability into physical spaces, responsible deployment requires ongoing governance beyond initial rollout — monitoring for robots picking up unwanted behaviors from customer or employee interactions including deliberate tampering , and treating privacy, safety guardrails geofencing, emergency stops , and bias in any ai driven allocation decisions as first order priorities rather than afterthoughts. the economist independently ai-project-selection-frameworks: summary three complementary frameworks for choosing which ai projects to pursue and how broadly to deploy them — a risk/demand 2x2 matrix for picking generative ai use cases, five traits of a strong first ai pilot, and the "deep and narrow" case against running dozens of shallow ai pilots at once. highlights a simple 2x2 matrix for picking generative ai use cases plots risk how likely and damaging would inaccurate or fabricated output be? against demand is there a real, sustainable need beyond current hype? — high demand/low risk use cases like marketing copy, corporate learning content, and text review/editing deserve immediate investment, while high risk/high demand cases medical diagnosis, legal advice, regulatory compliance will inevitably be slowed by warranted caution and regulation. a framework for picking the right generative ai project even a "low risk" quadrant use case like corporate learning still carries real risk — generative ai remains vulnerable to bias and factual errors just as humans are, so any output should be treated as a first iteration to refine with better prompts and human review, not distributed as finished work. a framework for picking the right generative ai project andrew ng's five traits of a strong first ai pilot project: it delivers a quick win ideally within 6 12 months, and running two to three parallel pilots raises the odds at least one succeeds significantly ; it's neither too trivial to matter nor too unwieldy to finish; it's specific to your own industry rather than a generic capability a larger competitor will out build; it can be accelerated with credible outside partners while an internal ai team is still being built; and it demonstrably creates value through one of three channels — cost reduction, revenue increase, or an entirely new line of business. how to choose your first ai project ai is better at automating discrete tasks than entire jobs — ng's example is a radiologist's job reading x rays, operating imaging equipment, consulting colleagues, surgical planning , where automating just one task like image reading is more tractable and realistic than automating the whole role — and a pilot needs a cross functional leader, a small team 5 15 people is typical , and deliberate internal celebration of milestones to build company wide momentum for further ai investment. how to choose your first ai project reckitt rejected a "shallow and broad" gen ai rollout many disconnected use cases across departments, each individually roi positive in favor of "deep and narrow": concentrating entirely on marketing, where insight generation, content creation, and product development are interlinked and reinforce each other, producing 60% faster product concept generation and 30%+ more efficient brand communications within two years. stop running so many ai pilots only 4% of companies take the deep and narrow, focused transformation approach according to a 2024 bcg survey of 1,000 cxos, but those that do achieve roughly double the roi over time of shallow and broad deployers — because deep and narrow forces genuine process reinvention change management is 70% of the challenge, versus 20% for data and 10% for the ai itself rather than bolting ai onto unchanged workflows. stop running so many ai pilots a four step process for choosing where to go deep: place candidate ai applications on a spectrum from office productivity routine, unlikely to create advantage through domain reinvention end to end process reimagination, the sweet spot for most firms to entirely new business models exciting but hard for some product categories ; target a domain that protects or extends an existing competitive strength l'oréal's beauty genius chatbot built on its skin biology research and decade of ar investment or amplifies one ikea using gen ai to make its design service scale and expertise advantage even more affordable ; prioritize efficiency gains before growth gains, since cost reduction is faster to realize and builds executive support for the harder growth bets; and systematically map every task in the target domain reckitt categorized 300 tasks across 2,000+ marketers by automation potential and opportunity size rather than picking use cases impressionistically. stop running so many ai pilots concept three frameworks, spanning different points in an organization's ai journey, address a shared underlying problem: how to decide which ai initiatives actually deserve investment, rather than chasing every plausible use case with equal enthusiasm. the earliest stage framework addresses the initial triage question for generative ai specifically — where should a company even start looking? — with a deliberately simple 2x2 matrix that plots risk how likely and how damaging would fabricated or inaccurate output actually be against demand is there a real, sustained need for this kind of output beyond the current hype cycle . the framework's core insight is that these two dimensions should be considered jointly rather than separately, since risk and demand both vary meaningfully across industries and functions: the high demand, low risk quadrant — marketing copy, internal learning content, text review and editing, brainstorming — is where investment should concentrate first, since the consequences of an error are limited a human typically reviews the output before it reaches a customer, or the content isn't fact heavy to begin with while genuine demand already exists. marketing illustrates this concretely: it requires constant idea generation, audience tailored messaging, and text rich content, is rarely fact dense in ways that create real risk, and already has abundant example content to prime a model with — which is exactly why several gen ai marketing copy startups reached unicorn status early in the technology's commercial life. the framework's caution is important, though: even in a nominally low risk quadrant like corporate learning, generative ai remains vulnerable to bias and factual error just as humans are, so any output should be treated as a first draft to refine through better prompting and genuine human review — not distributed at face value simply because the use case scored as low risk on the matrix. a framework for picking the right generative ai project once an organization has identified a plausible starting point, andrew ng's framework addresses a narrower and more tactical question: what makes a strong first ai pilot specifically, given that a pilot's purpose is only partly to create value — its more important job is convincing skeptical internal stakeholders to invest further in ai capability at all. five traits distinguish a well chosen pilot. it should deliver a quick win, ideally achievable within six to twelve months, and ng recommends running two or three parallel pilots rather than betting everything on one, since this materially raises the odds that at least one produces a clear success story. it should be sized correctly — neither so trivial that success wouldn't convince anyone the technology matters, nor so large and unwieldy that it risks stalling before it can prove anything. it should be specific to the organization's own industry rather than a generic capability, since a horizontal use case ng's example: a medical device company building an ai resume screening tool is likely to be outbuilt and undercut by a larger platform player serving many industries at once, and won't convince internal stakeholders that ai is worth investing in for their specific business either. it should be accelerated with credible external partners if the organization's own ai team is still being built, since waiting to build full in house capability before executing risks falling too far behind the technology's own pace of advancement. and it must demonstrably create value through one of three recognizable channels: reducing costs automation opportunities exist in nearly every industry , increasing revenue through recommendation and prediction systems , or enabling an entirely new line of business that wasn't previously possible. ng's own experience leading google brain illustrates the logic directly: rather than tackling web search or advertising google's most strategically central but politically fraught domains , his team's first internal customer was speech recognition, where a clear win built enough credibility to bring in google maps as a second project — each success compounding the next until google brain became central to google's broader ai transformation. practically, ng recommends treating ai as automation of discrete tasks rather than entire jobs a radiologist's job includes reading x rays, operating equipment, consulting colleagues, and surgical planning — automating just the reading task is far more tractable than automating "radiologist" wholesale , appointing a cross functional leader who bridges ai expertise and domain knowledge, keeping the team small 5 to 15 people is typical for a genuine pilot , conducting both business value and technical diligence before committing resources, and deliberately publicizing milestones internally talks, awards, even external pr so the pilot's success becomes visible enough to build company wide momentum, with credit shared generously with the business team specifically to encourage other business units to follow suit. how to choose your first ai project the third framework addresses a later stage failure mode: what happens once an organization has moved past initial pilots and is deciding how broadly to deploy gen ai across the business. the consumer packaged goods company reckitt illustrates the choice concretely — facing a long list of plausible, individually roi positive use cases spanning presentations, customer support, and procurement, its executives recognized that pursuing all of them would deliver only marginal, disconnected efficiency gains rather than genuine transformation, so they instead concentrated entirely on one domain, marketing, where gen ai could be applied across interconnected tasks insight generation, content creation, product development that reinforce each other — real time consumer insight feeding better product innovation, which in turn strengthens loyalty and advocacy. this "deep and narrow" approach produced measurable results within under two years: product concept generation 60 percent faster, and brand/marketing communication processes 30 percent or more efficient. the framework names the alternative — "shallow and broad," running many disconnected, individually justified use cases across departments — as not wrong exactly it does generate some genuine time and cost savings but structurally limited: when only 5 to 10 percent of tasks in any given function use gen ai, executives have little motivation to fundamentally rethink how that function operates, initiative fatigue sets in from too many disconnected pilots, and use cases that provide little real competitive advantage are easily copied by competitors, breeding employee skepticism over time. a 2024 bcg survey of 1,000 cxos found only 4 percent of companies actually pursue the harder deep and narrow path, but those that do achieve roughly double the roi of shallow and broad deployers over time — a gap the authors expect to widen further as ai capability continues advancing, since deep and narrow compounds structural, hard to copy advantage while shallow and broad mostly just captures easily replicated efficiency. the reason deep and narrow is harder, not merely different, is that it demands wholesale change management rather than incremental technology adoption: at reckitt, change management represented roughly 70 percent of the actual challenge, versus 20 percent for data readiness and just 10 percent for the ai technology itself. the framework offers a four step process for deciding where to go deep. first, place candidate applications on a spectrum from office productivity routine efficiency gains — summarizing meetings, drafting presentations — unlikely on their own to create competitive advantage through domain reinvention end to end reimagination of a function or process, the area of opportunity for almost any firm to entirely new business models exciting, but harder for companies whose core product doesn't lend itself easily to ai infusion, like toothpaste . second, target domains where deep ai deployment either protects or extends an existing competitive strength, or creates a new one that's genuinely hard to copy: l'oréal's beauty genius chatbot, which conducts an ai driven skin diagnosis and personalized product recommendation, works specifically because it draws on the company's decade of augmented reality investment and proprietary skin biology research — advantages a copycat chatbot simply can't replicate regardless of how good its underlying model is — while ikea used gen ai to amplify not replace its existing design service strength, letting professional designers complete projects in roughly 10 minutes that previously required paid consultants working over several days, leveraging ikea's uniquely large community of interior designers and correspondingly large volume of high quality training data. third, prioritize efficiency gains before growth gains within the chosen domain, since cost reduction is typically achievable faster than top line growth and helps build the executive confidence needed to greenlight the harder, slower to materialize growth bets that follow — exactly the sequence reckitt followed, demonstrating quick marketing efficiency wins media campaign analysis compressed from days to hours before its leadership authorized the longer horizon growth oriented gen ai work. fourth, systematically map the target domain's actual work rather than picking use cases by impression: reckitt catalogued all 300 distinct tasks its 2,000 plus global marketers performed, through both surveys and one on one interviews, then plotted each task by degree of possible automation and opportunity size to identify roughly 100 tasks genuinely suited to gen ai — a rigorous inventory process that also surfaced the reality that marketers' entire role, not just isolated tasks, would need reconsidering as gen ai absorbed routine work and freed people for more demanding responsibilities previously held by their managers. the organizing question throughout, whichever domain a company chooses, is whether a top competitor could replicate the resulting advantage using gen ai too — since the competitor doesn't need to match a company's underlying strength exactly, only to offer a "good enough," cheaper, simpler alternative to cause real damage, which is precisely the competitive logic deep and narrow deployment is designed to defend against. stop
