brand-trust-strategy-in-the-ai-era: summary brands face ai driven trust risk from three directions at once — a responsible ai expert panel says undisclosed ai use erodes customer trust before anything even goes wrong, seven years of consumer research shows five specific psychological pitfalls that turn an inevitable ai failure into disproportionate brand damage, and the rise of agentic commerce forces brands to compete for both human attention and ai agents' own recommendation logic through a genuinely new discipline — "share of model." highlights mit smr and bcg's third annual responsible ai expert panel found 84% of ai experts agree or strongly agree that companies should be required to disclose ai use to customers, framing disclosure as foundational transparency comparable to sustainability or nutritional labeling, and an ethical obligation enabling informed decision making and risk assessment — not just a legal compliance exercise. artificial intelligence disclosures are key to customer trust the panel converged on disclosure being most essential in two specific circumstances: when customers are directly interacting with an ai system rather than a human, and when ai is used in consequential decisions health care, finance, hiring — while agreeing that low stakes internal uses prioritizing emails, generating slides generally don't need disclosure, since demanding disclosure for every ai touched process would soon become impractical as ai becomes pervasive. artificial intelligence disclosures are key to customer trust after a cruise robotaxi's failure to disclose that it dragged an injured pedestrian 20 feet despite not being at fault for the initial collision triggered a $1.5 million regulatory fine, a criminal doj investigation, a revoked operating permit, 50% of the workforce laid off, the ceo's resignation, and more than 50% valuation loss, hbr's seven year consumer research program found five specific, controllable psychological pitfalls explain why ai failures cause disproportionate brand damage. don’t let an ai failure harm your brand pitfall 1 — people blame ai first: across a 5,000 participant study, respondents assigned more liability to a not at fault autonomous vehicle's maker than to an equivalent not at fault human driver, because novelty leads people to imagine an unrealistic "perfect driver" counterfactual the ai should have achieved; shifting attention toward the actually at fault human party reduces this bias, but deliberately hiding facts as cruise did backfires catastrophically once discovered. don’t let an ai failure harm your brand pitfall 2 — one ai's failure contaminates perception of all ai: a 3,724 participant study found people were more likely to predict an algorithm would fail in an unrelated state's benefit allocation system than a human employee would, because people treat "ai" as a homogeneous category rather than distinct systems with different capabilities — the defense is actively differentiating your ai anthropic markets claude's "constitutional" training approach specifically to dissociate it from competitors and disclosing human in the loop oversight, which reduces the assumption that one company's failure indicts ai generally. don’t let an ai failure harm your brand pitfall 3 — overstating ai capability increases blame when it fails: a 9,492 participant study found drivers using a vehicle labeled "autopilot" implying high capability took control later in a simulated crash than those using an identical vehicle labeled "copilot" implying midlevel capability , and companies using higher capability implying labels were judged more liable when failures occurred — meaning marketing campaigns that tout ai superiority like gm's "humans are terrible drivers" campaign for cruise can directly increase a company's own liability exposure. don’t let an ai failure harm your brand pitfall 4 — humanized ai gets judged more harshly for the same failure: studies found attitudes toward a brand were more negative when an investment loss "algorithm" was given a human name and persona "charles" than when described as a plain algorithm, since humanized bots get ascribed mental capabilities understanding, planning that increase perceived responsibility for failures — an effect that compounds with both verbal and visual humanlike cues, and that an analysis of roughly 500,000 customer chatbot sessions found gets specifically worse in situations involving already angry customers. don’t let an ai failure harm your brand pitfall 5 — people are outraged by ai systems with programmed group based preferences: after a mercedes benz executive said its self driving cars would prioritize passenger safety over pedestrians, the resulting media firestorm forced a public reversal; controlled studies confirmed people are far more outraged by any programmed preference favoring one demographic group over another than by a random decision in the same dilemma, while structural preferences prioritizing saving more lives, regardless of who they are draw far less backlash than group based ones. don’t let an ai failure harm your brand hbr's agentic commerce research identifies three coexisting modes of ai mediated brand consumer interaction: brand agents a company's own ai, like capital one's auto navigator chat concierge , consumer agents independent ai acting on the customer's behalf across brands, like claude's computer use shopping capability , and full ai intermediation both sides handled entirely by ai, like chatgpt's agent autonomously completing an opentable reservation . preparing your brand for agentic ai 60% of us shoppers surveyed expect to use agentic ai to complete purchases within 12 months, and consumer agents hold structural trust and data advantages over brand agents perceived as unbiased, fiduciary like advocates, and able to draw on cross brand behavioral data — but brands can offset this by leveraging proprietary, real time product data no general purpose agent can match sephora's ai, drawing on 140,000 skin tone color iq data and 34 million beauty insider profiles, drove 3x purchase completion and a 30% return reduction and by building human escalation paths servicenow's agent autonomously resolves 80% of queries and escalates the remaining 20%, cutting complex case resolution time 52% . preparing your brand for agentic ai pernod ricard discovered leading llms were miscategorizing its affordable ballantine's scotch as a "prestige" product, and launched a "share of model" monitoring program — regularly prompting popular ai models about its brands and iteratively adjusting website/advertising copy until the models' descriptions corrected themselves — a discipline other brands like danone are now adopting as the ai era successor to seo keyword optimization; one carnegie mellon study found even simple prompt wording changes shifted brand recommendation likelihood by as much as 78.3%. preparing your brand for agentic ai concept mit sloan management review and boston consulting group's third consecutive annual responsible ai expert panel — an international group of academics and practitioners assembled to gauge how organizations worldwide are implementing responsible ai — put a direct provocation to its panel of experts: should companies be required to disclose ai use in their products and offerings to customers? the response was close to consensus: 84% of experts agreed or strongly agreed. the panel's reasoning clustered around several reinforcing arguments. transparency, several experts argued, is the foundational precondition for any effective responsible ai framework and the most basic form of transparency required across virtually every domain of life — with several panelists explicitly comparing ai disclosure to existing product labeling norms for sustainability, climate impact, fair trade, or nutritional content, framing it as a natural extension of an established practice rather than a novel regulatory burden. beyond precedent, panelists argued companies have a genuine ethical obligation to disclose ai use specifically because it enables informed decision making and risk assessment — one panelist drew a direct analogy to disclosing a drug's side effects, arguing ai users have an equivalent right to know the risks hallucinations, fabricated sources associated with a tool before relying on it. beyond the ethical case, the panel noted concrete business reasons for disclosure even where not legally mandated: transparency helps build and sustain trust among customers, investors specifically screening for credible responsible ai governance, and employees who value working for a company with genuine rai commitments — meaning voluntary disclosure functions as a competitive differentiator, not merely a compliance cost. the panel was equally direct about disclosure's practical difficulties, however. several experts noted no clear, stable definition exists that reliably differentiates "ai" from ordinary software or decision making systems, making it genuinely hard to specify when disclosure is legally required in the first place; others warned that mandating disclosure without clearly specifying the particular harms it's meant to address risks producing vague, box checking compliance rather than genuine transparency, and that disclosures can inadvertently expose competitively sensitive information about a company's underlying models or training data. perhaps the panel's most consistent caution was that poor quality disclosure can actively undermine the transparency and accountability it's meant to serve: disclosures buried in dense terms of service language, or written in language ordinary customers can't parse, fail to accomplish their purpose regardless of whether they technically satisfy a legal requirement — several panelists specifically called for disclosures written in plain language and designed to be visually accessible at the actual point of interaction, not merely present somewhere in a legal document. the panel converged on a workable middle ground for when disclosure is actually necessary: most agreed disclosure should be required whenever a customer is directly interacting with an ai system rather than a human, and whenever ai is being used to make decisions of real consequence to a person's life health care, finance, hiring decisions were cited repeatedly , including disclosing how affected individuals can reach a human to challenge an ai driven decision or action. many panelists extended this to data specific disclosures as well — customers, several argued, have a right to know how their personal data is being used to train or operate the ai systems processing it, not just that ai is involved at all. at the same time, the panel was explicit that universal, blanket disclosure requirements would quickly become impractical as ai becomes genuinely pervasive across ordinary business operations — using ai to prioritize internal emails, point employees to open parking spaces, or draft slide decks was repeatedly cited as an example of ai use that doesn't warrant customer facing disclosure, in the same way companies don't disclose their use of a search engine or a mobile phone; the operative distinction several panelists drew was whether the ai use touches or profiles the customer directly which warrants disclosure versus purely internal operational use which generally doesn't . the panel's synthesized recommendations for organizations: ground disclosure decisions explicitly in core responsible ai principles like transparency and accountability rather than treating disclosure as a standalone legal checkbox; make disclosures genuinely easy to understand by engaging cross functional teams including ux/ui designers, not just legal drafters, so disclosures appear in the right place at the right moment rather than only in buried legal text; voluntarily go beyond whatever the applicable legal minimum happens to be, particularly wherever ai is making decisions of real consequence to individuals, since ethical obligation and legal requirement aren't the same threshold; and publish broader details of an organization's responsible ai program and code of conduct beyond narrow product level disclosures, since this builds trust with customers, investors, and employees simultaneously rather than only satisfying a narrow disclosure requirement for one specific product. artificial intelligence disclosures are key to customer trust where the mit smr/bcg panel addresses trust erosion before anything goes wrong, hbr's julian de freitas turns to the harder problem of managing brand damage once an ai system inevitably does fail — grounding the analysis in a stark real world case study. in october 2023, a general motors cruise robotaxi was involved in an accident in san francisco in which a human driven nissan struck a pedestrian who was then thrown into the autonomous vehicle's path; an independent engineering investigation found no human driver could plausibly have avoided the resulting collision, meaning cruise's vehicle genuinely wasn't at fault for the initial impact. but cruise's report to regulators omitted that the vehicle then dragged the severely injured pedestrian 20 feet, and when that omission surfaced, the fallout was severe and disproportionate to the underlying fault: a $1.5 million federal fine, a department of justice criminal investigation that ultimately produced a $500,000 settlement, revocation of cruise's san francisco operating permit, half the company's workforce laid off, the ceo's resignation, more than 50% of the company's valuation erased, a driverless waymo vehicle set on fire by an angry crowd in an unrelated incident, and regulatory investigations opened into multiple other av developers — culminating in gm ending its robotaxi business entirely by the end of 2024. drawing on seven years and seven separate research studies into how consumers perceive and react to ai failures, de freitas identifies five specific, empirically documented psychological pitfalls that together explain why ai failures generate this kind of disproportionate brand damage, and that marketers can actively manage rather than simply absorb as an unavoidable cost of deploying ai. first, people blame ai first: in a 5,000 participant study, respondents assigned significantly more liability to the maker of a not at fault autonomous vehicle than to an equivalent not at fault human driver in an identical accident scenario, a bias that has been independently replicated by researchers in china, suggesting it persists across cultural contexts. the mechanism, de freitas's research suggests, is that a novel technology like an av prompts people to imagine unrealistic counterfactuals — what a hypothetically perfect ai driver could have done — holding ai to a standard no human would be held to; deliberately shifting attention toward the actually at fault party measurably reduces this bias, but that tactic must not be confused with concealing genuinely relevant facts, since cruise's leadership emphasized the human driver's fault while omitting the dragging incident, and once that omission was discovered, the company lost control of the media narrative entirely and permanently damaged regulator trust in the process. second, one company's ai failure contaminates public perception of other companies' ai: in a study informing 3,724 participants about a benefit allocation error and randomly attributing it to either a human employee or an algorithm, participants were significantly more likely to predict that an algorithm rather than a human employee in an entirely unrelated state's system would make the same kind of error — a pattern the researchers replicated across multiple other ai failure scenarios, attributing it to people treating "ai" as a single homogeneous category rather than recognizing that different ai systems have genuinely different capabilities and failure modes this ripple effect showed up concretely after the cruise incident, when a waymo vehicle was attacked in an unrelated incident and regulators opened investigations into multiple other av companies that had nothing to do with the original accident . the available countermeasure is explicit differentiation: anthropic's marketing of claude specifically emphasizes its distinct "constitutional" training methodology precisely to dissociate the product from competitors and pre establish grounds for limiting contamination if a competitor fails, and companies that clearly communicate when a human supervises an ai system and retains final decision authority "human in the loop" also measurably reduce the odds that a given failure gets read as an indictment of ai in general. third, people place disproportionately more blame on companies that overstate their ai's capabilities: in a 9,492 participant study using driving simulations, participants using a vehicle labeled "autopilot" implying high capability took manual control significantly later in a simulated near collision than participants using an identically capable vehicle labeled "copilot" implying more modest, assistive capability — meaning the label itself induced complacency — and separately, participants consistently judged companies more liable for accidents when the company's own marketing had emphasized the ai's superior capability, directly implicating campaigns like gm's "humans are terrible drivers" advertising for cruise as a factor that may have increased, rather than decreased, the public's assignment of blame once an accident occurred. the practical corrective de freitas offers: companies using an inherently capability inflating label like "autopilot" should compensate by clearly and accurately explaining the system's true capabilities and limitations elsewhere — a website, fine print — since his research finds companies that pair a misleading label with clear supplementary disclosure face measurably fewer penalties after a failure than companies relying on the misleading label alone; the cleaner, if less marketing friendly, alternative is simply choosing an honestly calibrated label from the outset. fourth, people judge humanized ai systems more harshly for identical failures: in a study describing an investment allocation error as caused either by a plain "algorithm program" or by a named, humanized ai persona "charles" , brand attitudes were measurably more negative in the humanized condition — because humanized ai gets ascribed genuine mental capacities understanding, planning, remembering that in turn increase the perceived responsibility assigned to it when something goes wrong, an effect that compounds when both verbal cues first person language, a human name and visual cues a humanlike avatar are present together, and that a roughly 500,000 session analysis of a telecommunications company's chatbot interactions found gets specifically amplified when customers are already angry going into the interaction. the practical guidance is to reserve humanized bot personas for lower stakes, generally positive contexts product search, general assistance rather than deploying them in domains prone to angry customer interactions customer service complaints, billing disputes , and to proactively temper user expectations at the outset of an interaction the way slack's chatbot does "i try to be helpful. but i'm still just a bot. sorry!" , which research finds measurably reduces user frustration when the bot subsequently underperforms. fifth and finally, people are specifically outraged by ai systems with programmed group based preferences, distinct from ordinary ai error: after a mercedes benz executive stated the company's self driving cars would prioritize passenger safety over pedestrian safety if forced to choose, the resulting media firestorm forced a swift public reversal; de freitas's own controlled study, presenting 826 participants with autonomous vehicle dilemmas that were resolved either randomly or via a programmed group based preference favoring, say, a child over an elderly pedestrian , found participants were significantly more outraged by any programmed group based preference than by an equivalent random outcome — while a related study by other researchers found people are considerably more supportive of ai systems using structural preferences e.g., prioritizing saving a greater number of lives, regardless of who they are than group based ones, since a structural rule offers a clear, broadly agreeable utilitarian justification that a demographic based one does not. de freitas's overarching lesson is that ai failure is genuinely inevitable at scale, which makes proactive management of these five specific, empirically grounded risk factors — rather than simply hoping failure never occurs — the actual work of responsible ai marketing. don’t let an ai failure harm your brand a third hbr analysis, by oguz acar and david schweidel, addresses a distinct but closely related challenge: how brands must adapt not just to prevent ai driven trust damage, but to proactively compete for relevance as ai agents increasingly mediate the entire customer relationship. the starting example is instructive: pernod ricard's head of digital and design discovered, after partnering with a marketing agency to formally audit how leading ai models represented his liquor brands, that the models were often wrong or incomplete — one popular model, for instance, miscategorized the affordably priced ballantine's scotch as a "prestige" product. in response, pernod ricard launched an ongoing program to monitor and improve what the researchers call "share of model" — the measure of how often and how favorably a brand appears in ai generated results relative to its competitors — regularly prompting popular ai models with questions about its products, cataloging the responses, and iteratively adjusting website and advertising copy specifically to correct how the models describe its brands danone runs a comparable ongoing monitoring program . this shift, the authors argue, is the direct successor to the decades long discipline of search engine keyword optimization, now applied to an environment where a growing share of consumers research and increasingly complete purchases through ai intermediaries rather than traditional search: a july 2025 survey of 750 us consumers found 60% expect to use agentic ai to complete purchases within the next 12 months, and major platforms openai partnering with stripe, paypal, walmart, and shopify to enable in chat purchasing are actively building the infrastructure to make that shift concrete. the authors identify three coexisting, non mutually exclusive modes of ai mediated brand consumer interaction that companies must navigate simultaneously: brand agents, in which a company's own ai engages directly with customers capital one's auto navigator chat concierge can check dealership inventory, schedule test drives, and estimate trade in values, letting customers complete most of a car buying journey before ever visiting a dealership ; consumer agents, in which an independent ai acts on an individual's behalf across multiple brands claude's "computer use" capability navigating screens and completing purchases functions as something closer to a personal digital representative than a brand tool ; and full ai intermediation, in which agents interact autonomously on both sides of a transaction with minimal human involvement at all chatgpt's agent autonomously searching opentable, selecting a restaurant, and completing a reservation . to navigate this landscape, the authors propose a three stage adoption framework. stage one is determining whether deploying an ai agent makes sense at all for a given context, since research spanning 119,000 participants found consumer receptiveness to ai agents is high in low stakes, routine, predictable outcome domains illustrated by amazon's decade long evolution from the physical dash button through subscribe & save to the fully autonomous alexa+ ai, which can interpret an intent like "restock my groceries" and execute the full multistep task chain unassisted but notably lower in personally meaningful purchases, domains where visible human effort itself signals care gift giving, personal messages , high stakes decisions where people want to retain direct control healthcare, per boston university and salesforce survey research , subjective rather than objective judgment calls, and luxury or premium experiences where customers are explicitly paying for human guidance as part of the product itself lamborghini's ceo has deliberately resisted autonomous driving features specifically because the brand's value proposition is the visceral experience of driving, not being driven — the authors note this choice needn't be binary, illustrated by ag1's hybrid strategy of training its ai agent on brand voice and real time customer data for routine support interactions while keeping community building interactions like responding personally to every customer review strictly human, a program that achieved 99% ai agent interaction quality scores while measurably freeing human staff for complex, empathy requiring cases. stage two, once customers are receptive to ai agents generally, is persuading them to use a brand's own agent rather than an independent, third party alternative — a genuinely uphill battle, since consumer agents hold structural advantages in both perceived trust people naturally trust agents they personally control, viewing them as unbiased advocates analogous to a fiduciary financial adviser, whereas brand controlled agents are reasonably suspected of serving the company's interests over the customer's and data breadth an independent agent like chatgpt can draw on a user's accumulated history across every brand and domain, not just one company's data . the authors argue brands can offset this disadvantage by leveraging what independent agents structurally cannot replicate — deep, proprietary, real time product data sephora's ai draws on color iq technology differentiating 140,000 skin tones and first party profiles from more than 34 million beauty insider loyalty members, driving triple the purchase completion rate and a 30% reduction in returns and human in the loop escalation paths unavailable to a purely independent agent servicenow's agent autonomously resolves 80% of incoming queries and automatically escalates the remaining 20% to human experts, cutting complex case resolution time by 52% — while noting that responsible ai signaling itself measurably drives adoption: a salesforce survey found 72% of consumers demand transparency about whether they're interacting with ai or a human, and the authors' own three large scale discrete choice experiments with 3,268 uk participants found responsible ai features like privacy and auditability were consistently among the most influential factors in ai product adoption decisions — in one pension planning app study, embedding responsible ai features into the product design lifted predicted adoption from 2.4% to 63.2%. stage three addresses the reality that many consumers will nonetheless choose to rely on independent agents regardless of how well a brand's own agent performs, creating a distinct strategic imperative: ensuring a brand is visible to, and ultimately recommended by, those independent consumer agents. instacart's rapid, repeated adaptation illustrates the discipline required — building both an in app chatgpt powered search tool and a separate chatgpt plug in enabling users to add ingredients to a cart directly from a recipe conversation inside chatgpt itself, then launching a custom gpt when openai introduced that capability, maintaining presence across each new integration surface as the underlying platform evolved. harvard business school research the authors cite documents specific technical levers for shaping how ai agents perceive and recommend a brand, including "strategic text sequences" — algorithmically generated text, often nonsensical to human readers, added to a product page that measurably increased one fictional test brand's likelihood of being surfaced as an llm's top recommendation — and the emergence of next generation reasoning models that expose their own decision criteria, letting brands understand and align with the actual factors price, compatibility, reviews driving a given recommendation; separately, carnegie mellon research found that even simple prompt wording changes substituting synonyms in an otherwise identical query shifted brand recommendation likelihood by as much as 78.3%, underscoring that understanding how consumers actually phrase their ai queries — not just what products they're searching for — is now foundational to brand marketing content strategy. the authors also point to emerging technical standards brands are beginning to adopt proactively, particularly llms.txt, a machine readable format already used by cloudflare, hubspot, and stripe that structures product information specifically for ai agent parsing, with early adopters reporting measurable increases in both ai generated and organic traffic, and flag the likely future emergence of pay to play monetization models within ai mediated marketplaces analogous to search engine advertising, which will require brands to maintain visibility while navigating evolving transparency regulations around paid ai placement. preparing your brand for agentic ai related platform business models — the "share of model" discipline and agentic commerce brand strategy covered here are the brand side response to exactly the ai agent bypassing interfaces dynamic that concept describes eroding platforms' advertising and transaction fee revenue note: create this concept when that source is processed in a future batch agentic ai adoption and consolidation — pwc's finding there that trust in ai agents drops sharply for high stakes, autonomous use cases directly parallels this concept's finding that consumer receptivity to brand agents is lowest precisely in high stakes, personally meaningful, or luxury purchase domains open questions none of the three sources reconciles a direct tension between the disclosure panel's finding that ai use should be disclosed, especially for consequential decisions and the agentic brand strategy research's finding that brands should build "human in the loop" ceo-cyber-resilience-leadership: summary lessons from 37 ceo interviews on managing cyberattacks, drawn from research comparing executives who led their company through a serious breach against those who hadn't. covers the five regrets attack tested ceos share, and a seven part playbook for building organizational cyber resilience before an attack happens. highlights research based on 37 in depth interviews with ceos of large enterprises average revenue $12 billion across the us, europe, and asia — nine of whom had led their company through a serious cyberattack — allowing a direct comparison between battle tested and untested executive views on cybersecurity. the ceo’s cyber resilience playbook the most common regret: ceos overemphasized prevention whether an attack would happen over resilience when it would happen and how to respond , pouring resources into technological defenses while their organizations lacked basic organizational resilience practices — cyber resilience means minimizing an attack's impact, recovering quickly, and emerging stronger, not simply avoiding a breach. the ceo’s cyber resilience playbook four further regrets from ceos who had survived an attack: feeling merely accountable for cybersecurity rather than proactively responsible for it before anything went wrong despite 72% of all ceos surveyed admitting discomfort making cyber decisions ; blindly trusting cybersecurity teams without developing enough informed understanding to ask good questions or challenge advice; believing their organization was well prepared, a false confidence that bred complacency until an actual attack proved otherwise; and reacting to stakeholder pressure during a crisis rather than proactively reassuring shareholders, regulators, customers, and partners. the ceo’s cyber resilience playbook a ceo can play three distinct roles in reassuring stakeholders during a crisis: an amplifier reinforcing external pressure to create urgency and counter complacency , a filter judging which pressures to absorb versus pass on to the response team , or an absorber taking on pressure directly so it doesn't distract the people running recovery . the ceo’s cyber resilience playbook the resulting playbook has seven practices: bring in an outsider ceo with attack experience to brief leadership and the board; establish a recurring cyber resilience learning forum chaired by the ceo, ideally quarterly that sits outside formal risk governance and exists purely for shared understanding; commission an independent cyber resilience audit annually, treated like a financial audit, to build informed trust between the ceo and the technical team; identify the two to five business processes most critical to keeping the organization running, and map them to the systems that support them, before an attack forces the decision under pressure; line up outside expert assistance in advance legal, communications, forensics, ransom negotiation ; prepare a proactive crisis communications plan rather than going dark during an incident; and conduct a full organizational not just technical postmortem after any real attack. the ceo’s cyber resilience playbook surviving a serious cyberattack can also create genuine value: one ceo used the post attack technology consolidation to fund further resilience investment, and attacks often expose hidden process inefficiencies, deepen appreciation for previously invisible critical processes, and create opportunities to pull the organization together — including across competitors, since cyber resilience is a domain where even rival companies benefit from sharing lessons. the ceo’s cyber resilience playbook concept drawing on 37 in depth interviews with ceos of large enterprises averaging $12 billion in revenue across the us, europe, and asia — nine of whom had personally led their organization through a serious cyberattack — this research isolates what changes in a ceo's thinking once an attack has actually happened, by comparing their battle tested views against those of ceos who hadn't yet faced one. the clearest and most common regret among attack tested ceos was having overemphasized cybersecurity prevention at the expense of organizational resilience: these executives had focused on whether an attack would occur rather than when it would occur and how the organization would respond, pouring significant resources into technological defenses while lacking basic organizational resilience practices across departments. cyber resilience, as the ceos came to understand it only after being breached, is not about avoiding an attack but about an organization's capacity to anticipate, withstand, respond to, and adapt to one — minimizing impact, recovering quickly, and emerging stronger, since even the most technologically advanced organizations will eventually be breached and need to plan for that inevitability. the ceo’s cyber resilience playbook four further regrets rounded out the pattern. ceos who had lived through an attack regretted feeling merely accountable for cybersecurity — taking ownership only after something went wrong — rather than proactively responsible for it beforehand, a distinction that mattered enough that 72 percent of all ceos interviewed, attacked or not, admitted discomfort making decisions in the cyber domain; several described wanting to become "co responsible" alongside their ciso, a shift cisos in the same research welcomed since they had generally viewed their ceos as insufficiently engaged. related to this, ceos also regretted blindly trusting their cybersecurity and technology teams without building enough of their own understanding to ask informed questions or challenge advice — a gap that widened after an attack forced many ceos to leave the company's fate in the hands of experts whose reasoning they couldn't fully evaluate; the research found that the more ceos came to understand cyber resilience, the more concerned they became, and the more concerned they became, the more engaged they got. nearly all ceos without direct attack experience considered their organizations well prepared for one, a confidence that only the attack tested group recognized as dangerous complacency; even carefully built crisis playbooks, they noted, cannot capture how unpredictably a real attack unfolds, since attackers continually adapt and an incident may compromise the very infrastructure communication channels, for instance that a playbook assumes will still be available. finally, ceos regretted reacting to the barrage of competing stakeholder demands during a crisis — shareholders on financial impact, the board on recovery evidence, regulators on answers, customers on their data — rather than proactively reassuring those stakeholders, and the research identifies three distinct postures a ceo can take in that reassurance role: an amplifier who reinforces external pressure to maintain urgency, a filter who judges which pressures to pass through to the response team versus absorb, and an absorber who takes on stakeholder pressure directly so it doesn't distract the people actually running recovery. the ceo’s cyber resilience playbook from these regrets, the research distills a seven practice playbook for ceos to build resilience before an attack forces the lesson on them. bringing in an outsider ceo with direct attack experience to brief the leadership team and board provides a relatable wake up call that pure technologists can't replicate, since it comes from someone who has personally faced the same decisions. establishing a recurring cyber resilience learning forum — chaired by the ceo, held at least annually and ideally quarterly, deliberately separate from formal risk governance processes — builds shared understanding between business leaders and cyber experts and normalizes asking naive questions, which moves people toward the kind of informed trust the research found lacking. commissioning an independent cyber resilience audit annually, treated with the same seriousness as a financial audit, lets the ceo build informed trust with the technical team and surface organizational blind spots the ceo wouldn't otherwise see; the research notes cisos sometimes hesitate to propose this out of fear of being put on the spot, when in practice it tends to build trust and shared responsibility instead. identifying the two to five business processes most critical to keeping the organization running — and mapping them to the specific applications and servers that support them — needs to happen before an attack, since without this groundwork every department will insist its own processes are the ones that must be restored first, and decentralized decision making under crisis needs pre agreed priorities to avoid infighting. lining up expert assistance legal counsel for regulatory compliance, communications specialists, forensic investigators, and in the worst case ransom negotiators in advance, and preparing a proactive crisis communications plan rather than going dark during an incident, together prevent the ceo from having to build critical relationships and messaging for the first time under active crisis pressure — markets and regulators are notably less forgiving of organizations that appear to have been caught flat footed or seem to be hiding something. finally, conducting a full postmortem after any real attack — covering organizational resilience factors like communication and business continuity, not just technical root cause — often exposes outdated processes and inefficiencies that had gone unnoticed, and can become a genuine source of value: one ceo redirected savings from post attack technology consolidation directly into further resilience investment, while other ceos described the crisis creating new appreciation for previously invisible critical processes and opportunities to strengthen the organization more broadly, including through sharing lessons with peers and even competitors, since cyber resilience is a domain the research frames as fundamentally noncompetitive. the ceo’s cyber communicating through standardized apis — that is distinct from, and considerably more consequential than, simply running an existing application on cloud infrastructure. a microservice is designed to serve one narrow, well defined piece of application functionality, developed and deployed independently by a small team, and exposed to the rest of the system only through a defined api contract rather than through direct, tightly coupled dependencies. this independence yields four concrete benefits: development is simplified because small teams can focus on narrowly scoped, well understood code rather than navigating a sprawling monolith; changes become smaller and less risky, since modifying one microservice doesn't require reasoning about the entire application's dependency graph; individual services can be scaled up or down independently based on their own demand rather than forcing the whole application to scale as a single unit; and, because each microservice is fully tested and validated on its own, other teams building new applications can reuse an existing microservice with confidence, without needing to re validate it from scratch each time it's incorporated somewhere new. this is precisely why simply "lifting and shifting" an aging monolithic application into the cloud unchanged captures essentially none of the cloud's real advantage — the application still carries the same tangled dependencies and inefficiencies it had on premises, and the genuine economic and agility benefit of the cloud comes specifically from decomposing an application into modular, independently deployable services, not from relocating existing code to different hardware. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.6 a closer look at cloud services containers are the packaging mechanism that makes microservices practical at scale, and they extend a layer of abstraction that virtual machines had already begun. a virtual machine abstracts away the physical server: multiple vms can share one physical machine while each runs its own complete, isolated operating system, letting an organization avoid dedicating a whole physical server to every individual application or experiment. a container goes a step further by abstracting away the operating system itself — a container packages an application's code together with all of its dependencies encapsulation so it can run predictably across different environments without needing to carry an entire os along with it, which is why containers are dramatically smaller and faster to start than vms, and why code can move confidently between a developer's desktop, a vm, and a public cloud without the "it worked on my machine" class of failure that plagued earlier deployment models. because a single real world application is commonly composed of hundreds or thousands of individual containers, managing them by hand is impractical, which is the specific problem container orchestration platforms exist to solve — automating the installation, scaling, health monitoring, versioning, and update rollout of containerized applications across a cluster of machines. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.6 a closer look at cloud services kubernetes, created by engineers at google and open sourced in 2014, has become the dominant container orchestration platform, having outcompeted alternatives docker swarm, apache mesos, cloud specific options like amazon ecs largely on the strength of its functionality, its large and rapidly growing open source ecosystem monitoring via prometheus, service meshing via istio, and many others , and — critically — its portability across public cloud providers, private clouds, and on premises infrastructure alike, which directly helps organizations avoid vendor lock in to any single cloud provider. kubernetes automates core operational concerns that would otherwise require substantial manual effort: standardized application build, packaging, deployment, and execution regardless of the underlying language; horizontal auto scaling that spins up additional instances as demand grows; high availability through continual health checks on nodes and containers; constructive-disagreement-language: summary research showing that observable language, not private intentions, determines whether a workplace disagreement stays constructive. covers the intention behavior and behavior perception gaps that undermine good intentions, five specific linguistic techniques, and how organizations can train, measure, and hire for this skill. highlights a 1,113 person study found that people instructed on the specific words and phrases to use when expressing receptiveness to an opposing view were rated by their disagreement counterparts as more objective, intelligent, and trustworthy — and counterparts were more willing to work with them in future — than people who received either no guidance or the classic "consider the other side's perspective and be empathetic" advice, since only concrete language actually produced observable, judgeable behavior. a smarter way to disagree the intention behavior gap explains why good intentions alone fail: even people who genuinely intend to be curious and respectful often can't sustain it under the emotional pressure of active disagreement — in the researchers' studies, participants who agreed that expressing curiosity was a good idea nonetheless defaulted to disguised argument making, such as asking "how can you believe that?" as if it were a genuine question. a smarter way to disagree the behavior perception gap means that even successfully executed intended behaviors aren't always read as intended by the other person — a question meant to signal curiosity "why would you think that?" can land as a sarcastic taunt, and the researchers found a consistent disconnect between how curious/receptive speakers rated their own messages and how curious/receptive readers actually rated the same messages. a smarter way to disagree five specific linguistic techniques, developed and tested across a decade of experiments, close both gaps: state curiosity directly "i'm curious how you think about xyz" rather than implying it through rhetorical questions; acknowledge the other side by restating the core of their position before responding, proving you were listening even without agreeing; make common ground explicit "we both want…" since some shared basis almost always exists even amid sharp disagreement; hedge claims "from my view…" rather than asserting certainty, since the average person is wrong at least half the time in factual disputes and hedging reads as more thoughtful, not weaker; and share a personal story behind a belief, since vulnerability built trust more effectively than citing research or data in a controlled bonus allocation experiment. a smarter way to disagree language, not nonverbal behavior, is the right lever for organizational intervention, since most professional communication today happens in writing email, slack, text where nonverbal cues don't even apply, and language is inherently easier to control and less prone to misinterpretation than tone or body language, even though words themselves can still be misread. a smarter way to disagree organizations can operationalize this in four ways: teach explicit verbal skills rather than abstract mindset advice train "express curiosity verbally" instead of just "be curious" ; have leaders model the specific behaviors in team meetings, one on ones, and town halls, since conversational receptiveness is contagious — people treated respectfully during disagreement tend to respond in kind; use technology nlp toxicity monitors, post conversation feedback dashboards, ai chatbot practice partners to measure and reinforce the right language at scale, noting employees are often more willing to practice disagreement with an ai than with a real colleague or boss; and factor constructive disagreement skill into hiring and promotion the same way other soft skills are assessed, following harvard's approach of asking applicants to describe how they handled a real disagreement. a smarter way to disagree concept disagreement is both valuable and risky in organizational life: divergent perspectives spark creativity, catch costly errors, and improve decisions, but disagreement handled poorly carries real interpersonal and financial costs — and despite decades of advice from academics and consultants, conflict in organizations persists. much of that advice has historically targeted internal mental states: "put yourself in their shoes," "have compassion and empathy," "try to understand rather than judge." a decade of experimental research finds this approach has a fundamental limitation — people cannot read each other's minds, so unless an internal mental state gets translated into something observable, it has essentially no effect on how a disagreement actually unfolds. this was demonstrated directly in a study of 1,113 people writing messages to someone who strongly disagreed with them about a hiring policy: participants who received no guidance, participants who received classic perspective taking and empathy guidance, and participants given specific words and phrases to signal receptiveness were compared, and only the third group — trained on concrete language — was rated by their disagreement counterparts as more objective, intelligent, and trustworthy, and as someone they'd be more willing to work with again. the implication is that organizations should focus training on observable linguistic behavior specifically, not general mindset coaching, because language unlike thoughts and feelings can actually be seen, measured, and improved by others — counterparts, trainers, mentors, or technology. a smarter way to disagree two specific gaps explain why good intentions so often fail to produce constructive disagreement in practice. the intention behavior gap is the same phenomenon behind failed new year's resolutions: even a genuine intention to stay curious and respectful collapses under the real pressure of active conflict, especially when someone is directly contradicting a deeply held belief. in the researchers' studies, participants overwhelmingly agreed in principle that expressing curiosity toward an opposing view was the right approach, yet when actually asked to do it, they frequently failed — getting pulled back into making their own argument, or disguising an argument as a rhetorical question "can you honestly say you think that is a good idea?" rather than genuinely signaling openness. the behavior perception gap is a second, independent failure mode: even when someone successfully executes their intended behavior, there's no guarantee the other party interprets it as intended, since ultimately the listener — not the speaker — determines how a message comes across. a question meant to convey genuine curiosity "why would you think that?" can easily be heard as a sarcastic jab instead, and the research documented a consistent disconnect between how curious and receptive message writers rated their own communications and how curious and receptive the actual readers rated those same messages. closing both gaps together requires organizations to help people learn behaviors that will actually be interpreted as intended, and then to help them successfully execute those specific behaviors under real conflict pressure — a two part problem that vague mindset advice alone cannot solve. a smarter way to disagree five specific, research tested linguistic techniques address this directly, all sharing a common thread: they use language to escape the competitive spiral that disagreements tend to fall into, and each requires the speaker to express a degree of vulnerability that instinct usually resists. signaling curiosity directly and explicitly "hey, it seems we're seeing this differently — i'm curious how you think about xyz" works better than implying interest through indirect or rhetorical questions, and doesn't require abandoning one's own position in the process "i believe xyz, but i'd love to understand where you're coming from" . acknowledging the other side by restating the core of their statement — even without agreeing with it — proves genuine listening and gives the other person confidence their message actually registered "i hear you — the team has been working really long hours, and this is a demanding client. but here's why we can't add more staff..." . finding common ground by explicitly naming shared beliefs, values, or goals "i agree with some of what you're saying…," "we both want…" counters the tendency for a specific point of disagreement to consume all attention even when broader alignment exists. hedging claims — using language like "from my view…" or "sometimes it is the case…" rather than asserting flat certainty — is grounded in the finding that in factual disagreements like a project's cost or a technical glitch's cause , the average person is wrong at least half the time, and research has shown that people who acknowledge a complex issue has multiple sides are perceived as more thoughtful and knowledgeable than people who make dogmatic claims that later turn out false. and sharing a personal story behind a belief builds trust more effectively than leaning on data or research alone, since people's strongest convictions typically trace back to lived experience rather than a slide deck — in one controlled experiment, participants entrusted with dividing a shared bonus after hearing others' positions trusted more those who shared a vulnerable personal story than those who cited research results. a smarter way to disagree the article specifically recommends focusing organizational effort on language rather than nonverbal behavior like eye contact or posture, for two practical reasons: a large share of today's professional communication already happens in writing email, slack, text , where nonverbal signals don't apply at all, and even in verbal exchanges, language is both easier to deliberately control and less prone to misinterpretation than nonverbal cues, which can inflect meaning in ways speakers don't intend. this doesn't mean mindset coaching is worthless — any successful organizational intervention still needs employee buy in, and someone who genuinely doesn't want to show empathy or curiosity will resist behavioral coaching regardless — but mindset advice should always be paired with concrete guidance on how to actually express that mindset in words, not left as an abstract aspiration. concretely, organizations have four levers available. they can teach specific verbal skills directly, replacing vague instructions "be curious," "be open minded" with trained behaviors expressing curiosity verbally, practicing conversational receptiveness, learning effective storytelling . they can have leaders model these exact behaviors in the organization's regular rhythms — team meetings, one on ones, performance evaluations, town halls — since the research finds conversational receptiveness is contagious, meaning people treated with respect during disagreement tend to respond in kind, reinforcing the behavior across the organization over time. they can use technology to reinforce the change at scale: many organizations already run nlp based toxicity monitoring on digital conversations, but the more valuable application is proactive rather than reactive — preconversation reminders of useful phrases, dashboards giving employees direct feedback on their own conversational behavior immediately after an interaction, and generative ai powered chatbots that let employees practice disagreement language and receive specific feedback, which is especially useful since people are typically more willing to disagree openly with an ai than with a real colleague or manager, given the lower relationship risk. and they can factor constructive disagreement skill directly into hiring and promotion decisions, the same way organizations already weigh other soft skills like teamwork — harvard and several other top universities now require applicants to describe a strong disagreement they navigated and how they handled it, a model that translates directly into hiring interviews and performance evaluations for constructive disagreement ability specifically. a smarter way to disagree related team based ai risk judgment — the forrester's survey research paints a picture of genuine mismatch between how eagerly companies pursue personalization and how consumers actually experience it. personalization is often equated by consumers with intrusive marketing rather than genuine service — one research participant described it bluntly as coming "with privacy violations," while another wanted brands to simply "leave me be." this resistance concentrates specifically at the start of the customer relationship: 54 percent of us online adults are unwilling to share personal information in exchange for more relevant advertising, and only 27 percent want personalized emails at all, with individualized messaging facing the most pushback in the early discover, evaluate, and commit stages before any real relationship exists. that resistance softens meaningfully once trust is established — 42 percent of us online adults consider personalized experiences an important part of loyalty programs specifically, and consumer comfort with data sharing varies sharply by how sensitive the information involved actually is: only 12 percent of people who recently opened a bank account want personalized banking advice, compared to 28 percent willing to share information for a better retail shopping experience, since financial services and healthcare carry inherently more sensitive data than retail. the strategic implication is that companies overinvesting in aggressive personalization early in the customer lifecycle, before any relationship exists to justify it, are working directly against the grain of consumer sentiment — the deeper, more individualized forms of personalization are something companies need to earn through demonstrated value, not something they can front load. the state of consumer personalization, 2022 getting the strategy right starts with defining what depth of personalization is actually appropriate for a given moment, since not every customer interaction warrants the same level of individualization. forrester lays out a spectrum running from segmentation bucketing customers into broad, predefined groups — the most established approach, dating back decades, and still the right tool for many use cases , through discrete interactions single moment, next best offer or next best action suggestions triggered by one specific action, like a browsed product prompting a related recommendation , to preset personas or customer determined journeys mapping a customer into an ongoing track — a beauty brand's "dry skin" persona, or a car seat maker's "toddler" life stage — that shapes an extended sequence of future communications , up to contextual understanding that anticipates individual needs in real time, the deepest and most demanding form, formalized under the separate concept of next best experience nbx and requiring real time interaction management technology to actually deliver. rather than jumping straight to "what data do we need" and "what tech should we buy," forrester insists strategy has to come first, structured around four questions asked in a specific order: what does the consumer actually need grounded in real customer research rather than internal assumption, since "we can personalize, so we should" is explicitly rejected as a justification ; what is the specific business objective and its measurable kpi, defined only after the consumer need is established; what is the specific tactic, and at which point or points in the customer lifecycle it should apply, whether as a single tactic at one stage or several tactics orchestrated across the whole journey; and who needs to be involved, since personalization sits inside customer insights, data and analytics, crm, it, and marketing simultaneously — meaning that, in practice, everyone owns personalization and yet no single function truly owns it, a genuine organizational paradox that has to be resolved deliberately rather than left to default to whichever team happens to control the budget. a strategy guide to consumer personalization if strategy is personalization's blueprint, data is its fuel — and forrester organizes consumer data along two independent axes. the first axis is provenance and degree of customer "knownness": zero party data is the most valuable and rarest type, proactively and explicitly volunteered by the customer preference center selections, stated purchase intentions, personal context, and how they want to be recognized , inherently signaling permission and intimacy; first party data is a company's own directly collected transactional, demographic, behavioral, and implied interest data time on a product page, apps frequented, loyalty and customer service activity , generally making a customer more known than unknown across their history with the company; second party data results from two companies deliberately combining their respective customer data sets under partnership a financial services firm and a retailer cross referencing which household income bands correlate with certain purchases, for instance ; and third party data, purchased or licensed from outside sources like affinity segments or contextual data, is explicitly described as falling out of favor as data deprecation and privacy regulation intensify. the second, independent axis is data frequency: static data birth date, gender, parental status, mailing address updates rarely enough that refresh speed barely matters, and is used to build defined audience segments; dynamic data location, temperature, energy consumption, biometric activity must be captured and acted on in near real time or genuinely real time, and is what actually triggers a specific personalized moment rather than merely defining who's eligible for one. in practice, forrester finds companies running into the same three failure modes repeatedly, often simultaneously: missing data, where a needed attribute simply isn't captured, turning what should be a quick test into an entirely new data collection and crm schema project; siloed data, where departmental and even within department silos a classic example being social media learning a preference that never reaches crm or the email team prevent any single, complete view of the customer from forming; and non actionable data, where information does get centrally aggregated but remains too stale, disjointed, or unclean to actually drive real time or near real time decisions. these problems are intensifying rather than easing: 80 percent of b2c cmos surveyed said rising consumer privacy protections are actively changing their view of what marketing personalization can even involve, up sharply from 45 percent just two quarters earlier — meaning the practical data foundation for personalization is getting harder to build even as strategic ambition for it grows. forrester's recommended sequence for tackling this is to identify exactly what data a specific tactic requires, locate where that data currently lives across the organization's inevitable silos, build a concrete plan to access and activate it respecting each data owner's governance and integrity requirements along the way , and finally verify data quality, since running personalization off unreliable or improperly matched "unknown person" data produces measurably less accurate results than personalization built on properly resolved, first party data. a data primer for consumer personalization even with strategy and data in place, execution demands technology — but forrester is explicit that there is no single "personalization technology" category to buy: personalization capability is instead scattered across many overlapping technology categories, and only 19 percent of b2c marketers who use enterprise marketing technology believe a single vendor can supply everything they need, with the average program stitching together roughly eight discrete technologies. forrester organizes the technology landscape into five functional categories that any complete personalization stack must cover, whether through one platform or several coordinated ones. recognition technology pinpoints who the customer actually is, spanning customer data platforms which unify contact information, purchase history, and preferences, though typically incompletely , zero party data and preference center solutions, identity resolution tools that link a customer's identifiers across channels and devices, and journey mapping platforms — an area where "creating a single view of the customer across channels" remains, per forrester's own 2023 survey data, among b2c marketers' top execution challenges. insights technology turns that recognized data into understanding of the customer's context — journey stage, behavior, intent — via customer analytics, journey analytics, and digital intelligence platforms, aiming toward the ideal of next best experience decision making grounded in everything known about a customer rather than a short term sales driven heuristic. decisioning technology is where that understanding actually becomes a specific next best offer, action, or experience determination, spanning the full range from simple rules based logic through machine learning and ai driven models, real time interaction management rtim systems, creative adtech that dynamically assembles and tests ad variants, and customer journey orchestration platforms that adjust a customer's path in near real time based on their behavior. delivery technology is personalization's "last mile," the channel specific and cross channel tools — advertising technology, cross channel marketing hubs, commerce technology, and customer service platforms — that actually execute an interaction across email, sms, app, website, social, in store, or contact center touchpoints, each with its own formatting requirements and quirks. and optimization technology runs continuously in the background across marketing resource management, marketing measurement and optimization, and experience optimization platforms, closing the feedback loop by measuring both customer facing value like net promoter score and business value like incremental sales to continually refine future insights and decisioning — sometimes using reinforcement learning to improve decisioning models automatically over time. given this fragmentation, forrester's recommended vendor vetting checklist asks which of the five functional categories a given tool genuinely supports as opposed to its marketing language ; what depth of personalization it can actually execute, matched against the organization's own data maturity and business goals; what level of identity resolution it achieves, since not every use case simple segmentation, for instance actually requires full resolution; how automated its decisioning genuinely is, with an explicit warning to be skeptical of vendors overpromising ai, since rules based decisioning remains "omnipresent" underneath much of what's marketed as ai driven, and human supervision of any automation remains necessary; how it measures and optimizes personalization's impact, blending customer facing and company facing metrics; and to what degree it actually integrates with the rest of the organization's cx, marketing, sales, commerce, and customer service technology ecosystem, since deeper integration is generally preferable but not always necessary depending on how much and how quickly data genuinely needs to flow between systems. a technology overview of including its critique of the narrower next best product/offer/action trilogy this concept's "decisioning" technology category still largely relies on data governance strategy — the data silo and data quality failure modes documented here are specific instances of the broader enterprise data management discipline covered there enterprise data risk management — the privacy and consent pressures shaping this concept's zero/first/second/third party data taxonomy are a direct application of that concept's data protection and data compliance risk categories open questions the sources don't reconcile how a company should sequence investment across the five technology categories when budget is limited — whether, for instance, recognition data foundation should always precede decisioning the more visible, roi attributable layer in practice. sources the state of consumer personalization, 2022 — forrester's consumer sentiment survey data on personalization resistance across the customer
