company specific applications an hr onboarding chatbot, for example . the researchers caution that american ai companies dismiss the chinese llm disruption threat, or the parallel threat from resource light small language models, at their own peril — self disruption deliberately cannibalizing one's own premium offering with a cheaper alternative, as ge did by developing its own lower cost handheld ultrasound device is a theoretically available defense but empirically very difficult to execute, not least because sunk costs already invested in expensive chips, hardware, and training data, plus strong incentives to keep selling high margin solutions, tend to tether incumbent companies to their existing high end offerings rather than cannibalizing them proactively. why deepseek shouldn’t have been a surprise much of the initial deepseek coverage carried an undertone of accusation — specifically, that deepseek had obtained proprietary knowledge from openai's closed source o1 model without permission via a technique called distillation, framed by much of the press as evidence deepseek had discovered some new, illicit shortcut to efficient ai. quanta magazine's explainer corrects this framing directly: knowledge distillation, in which a smaller "student" model is trained to approximate a larger "teacher" model's behavior at a fraction of the cost, is a decade old, extremely well established technique in ai research, not a novel or inherently improper one — "one of the most important tools that companies have today to make models more efficient," in the words of one researcher who studies the technique. the idea traces to a 2015 paper by three google researchers, including geoffrey hinton later a 2024 nobel laureate , who were seeking a more efficient alternative to the then common practice of running expensive "ensembles" of multiple models glued together to improve performance. their key insight was that a model's wrong answers aren't all equally wrong — confusing a dog with a fox is a smaller error than confusing a dog with a pizza — and that a large "teacher" model's full probability distribution across possible answers its "soft targets," which hinton evocatively called "dark knowledge," by analogy to cosmological dark matter contains far richer information than just its single best answer. by training a smaller "student" model on these soft targets rather than only on hard, final answers, researchers found they could compress a large, complex model down to a much leaner one with barely any loss of accuracy. the technique wasn't an immediate hit — the original paper was initially rejected from a conference — but it arrived at exactly the moment neural networks were exploding in size and cost as researchers discovered more training data reliably improved performance; google's 2018 bert language model, powering billions of web searches but expensive to run at scale, was itself distilled into the smaller, widely adopted distilbert the following year, and distillation is now offered as a managed service by google, openai, and amazon alike, with the original 2015 paper cited more than 25,000 times. crucially, distillation in its classic form requires access to a teacher model's internal probability outputs, which makes the specific accusation against deepseek — that it covertly distilled openai's fully closed source o1 model without permission — technically implausible in the traditional sense; what remains genuinely possible, and much harder to detect or prevent, is a "socratic" variant in which a student model is trained purely on a teacher model's answers to systematically prompted questions, without ever touching the teacher's internals. the technique's ongoing relevance extends well beyond the deepseek controversy: researchers at uc berkeley's novasky lab recently showed distillation works effectively even for training complex chain of thought reasoning models multistep "thinking" systems built to answer harder questions , producing their fully open source sky t1 model for under $450 in training cost while achieving results comparable to a much larger open source model — evidence, as one of the researchers put it, that "distillation is a fundamental technique in ai," not a shortcut peculiar to any one company or country. how distillation makes ai models smaller and cheaper a later hbr analysis, published after the initial deepseek shock had settled into sustained strategic attention, argues that deepseek is best understood as one visible instance of a much larger, deliberately distinct chinese generative ai ecosystem — not an isolated anomaly to be reacted to and then set aside. drawing on executive interviews, performance benchmarks, and case studies conducted at imd, the researchers propose a "3c framework" distinguishing this ecosystem across the three layers of the gen ai stack infrastructure, intelligence/llms, and application/output : customization, cost leadership, and calibration. customization in infrastructure reflects chinese firms' preference for vertically integrated, end to end technology stacks over the more decentralized, multi vendor ecosystem typical of us ai development — huawei, for instance, built its own deep learning framework, mindspore, specifically to run on its own ascend ai chips, giving it lower cost customization ability than a company assembling ai capability from disparate, generalized vendors; ant group's ai doctor agents, available through its alipay app, illustrate the same principle applied to an entire vertical, trained not just on clinical literature and structured diagnostic data but explicitly on the decision making logic of top chinese physicians, achieving a contextual depth general purpose models like chatgpt struggle to match. cost leadership in model development reflects a genuine mindset difference the researchers observed repeatedly in interviews: where western firms tend to pursue cutting edge infrastructure and models on the theory that business results will eventually follow, chinese firms more often treat models and infrastructure explicitly as a means to a predetermined business outcome, leaning on mature existing ai solutions rather than building from scratch wherever feasible — a mindset made viable by china's vast domestic market and its handful of centralized ai solution suppliers, and one the researchers note has been aided by chinese firms directly observing both the successes and the costly failures of western competitors like openai, google, and meta along the way. calibration for real world applications reflects an obsession with practical effectiveness over theoretical elegance, illustrated by moonshot ai's kimi model, which in march 2024 became the first ai system to process up to 2 million chinese characters within a single conversation — a milestone the researchers frame not as a narrow technical achievement but as a capability deliberately calibrated for document heavy real world use cases across healthcare, education, and customer service. this entire ecosystem, the researchers note, developed against a backdrop of intensifying export controls specifically intended to constrain it — controls that instead appear to have catalyzed rather than crippled chinese ai development: more than 300 gen ai services are now registered with the cyberspace administration of china, and huawei fast tracked its homegrown ascend chip series specifically as a domestic alternative to restricted nvidia hardware, with ascend chips now powering national scale chinese data centers. for global executives, the researchers' central recommendation is a deliberate "dual track" strategy rather than viewing the choice as east versus west: western tools remain well suited to general purpose research and maximum flexibility, while chinese tools increasingly offer superior cost efficiency, faster deployment, and better real world calibration for domain specific applications — but pursuing this dual track approach requires navigating genuine complexity, since western technology and infrastructure are already difficult to access within china, and chinese ai vendors face rising scrutiny in the us, requiring more rigorous due diligence spanning chip sourcing reviews, cybersecurity audits, and alignment with evolving local ai governance requirements on both sides. how savvy companies are using chinese ai related enterprise ai token cost management — the price differential this concept documents between chinese and western llms as low as $0.30 vs. $60+ per million output tokens is a direct input into the model rightsizing and portfolio pricing strategies that concept recommends for managing enterprise token spend ai vendor pricing and profitability — deepseek's cost efficiency breakthrough directly undercuts andy wu's argument there that high inference costs structurally constrain ai vendor profitability, suggesting the cost floor for capable models may be considerably lower than western labs' spending implied open questions none of the four sources addresses how durable deepseek's specific cost advantage is likely to prove as western labs adopt similar efficiency techniques mixture of experts, distillation themselves — it's unclear whether the cost gap between chinese and western frontier models will persist, narrow, or reverse over the following months and years. the "plural governance" and "dual track" strategic recommendations from the two hbr pieces aren't reconciled with the data privacy and cross border regulatory concerns both pieces separately raise — neither source specifies how a company should decide which specific workflows are safe to route to a chinese llm provider versus which carry unacceptable data sovereignty risk. sources what is deepseek and how is it upending a.i. — the new york times' explainer on deepseek's january 2025 release, framework for enterprise llm strategy. how distillation makes ai models smaller and cheaper — quanta magazine's explainer on knowledge distillation, its 2015 origins, and its role in the digital-value-chain-unbundling: summary api driven digital integration lets firms embed hyperspecialized third party services directly into their operations rather than merely outsourcing tasks, giving rise to "orchestrators" that coordinate an end to end offering from many narrow providers. this reconfigures value chains — lowering barriers to entry, opening new distribution and monetization channels, and sometimes turning yesterday's specialist partner into today's direct competitor. highlights today's unbundling differs from decades of traditional outsourcing in one crucial way: instead of handing a task off to a third party, firms embed external hyperspecialized services directly into their own operations via apis — cloud based logistics platform shipbob lets small brands offer two day shipping without building fulfillment infrastructure, and cloud kitchen network kitopi lets a "restaurant" consist of just a brand, recipes, and menus with everything else outsourced. two forces enabled this wave: the digitization of customer facing workflows domino's online orders — over 85% of u.s. retail sales — automatically trigger in store cooking schedule coordination created the internal integration that made external integration a natural next step; and the spread of standardized digital interfaces, especially apis, which now power the majority of internet traffic and let firms discover and integrate services through public directories like postman 100,000+ listed apis . hyperspecialized providers capture scale economies unavailable to any single client — shipbob spreads fixed warehouse and transportation costs across millions of orders from thousands of businesses, and can absorb demand spikes for one client by rebalancing capacity across its whole network — democratizing access to infrastructure and expertise once reserved for industry giants an aspiring chef can launch a restaurant with no physical location using cloud kitchens, uber eats, and stripe . "orchestrators" — companies that coordinate the end to end workflow and serve as the customer's primary point of contact without controlling every underlying capability, exemplified by uber eats — create genuinely new distribution channels: embedding insurance purchases directly into travel or ticketing expedia, ticketmaster, uber is projected to make embedded channels 30% of all insurance transactions within five years, up from a historically low adoption, cumbersome to buy product category. digital integration unlocks new monetization for previously idle assets: flexe lets businesses rent out excess warehouse capacity, wareclouds turns private homes into distribution centers, and virtual dining concepts connects delivery only restaurant brands with unused kitchen capacity — the same underlying pattern walmart applied at incumbent scale by opening its logistics infrastructure to third party sellers through walmart fulfillment services. the reconfiguration cuts both ways: established players must watch orchestrator partners become direct competitors, as when food delivery platform glovo initially just coordinating grocery partner inventory began investing in its own "dark stores" to compete directly with the grocery chains it once served, and kitopi moved from partnering with restaurants to launching its own virtual restaurant brands. a four step playbook for preparing a company for this shift: digitize internal processes around apis target's store pickup model, zara's rfid tagged inventory so external integration becomes a natural extension rather than a separate project; catalog the external services relevant to your industry using public api directories and marketplace platforms shopify's 8,000+ app store, insurance specific heraldapi ; decide what to unbundle by weighing which tasks benefit most from external scale/expertise against the risk of losing internal synergies and the operational risk of dependency synapse financial technologies' 2024 collapse stranded the fintech startups that had outsourced their banking backend to it ; and decide whether to open your own systems and assets to others as a new revenue stream shopify's third party app ecosystem, walmart's logistics as a service . ai and end to end integrated ecosystems are identified as the next amplifiers of this trend: maersk feeds real time sensor, gps, and partner data into ai systems that optimize global shipping routes and coordinate with port authorities and customs agencies through the same digital interfaces that enable hyperspecialization elsewhere; fast fashion retailer shein compressed its design to market cycle from three weeks to five days through a fully digitized, ai informed supply chain, and is now packaging that same infrastructure as a "supply chain as a service" offering for external brands — the orchestrator pattern applied reflexively to its own operating capability. autonomous agentic ai is flagged as a likely accelerant still in its early stages: unlike today's largely human triggered api integrations, agentic systems embedded within and across company workflows could learn, adapt, and make sourcing, scheduling, and logistics decisions independently in response to real time conditions, a capability fedex is already deploying to optimize delivery route decisions from real time transportation and external condition data. concept how tasks to specialist firms — has entered a qualitatively different phase driven by digital integration technologies, above all apis. the crucial distinction from traditional outsourcing is that firms no longer simply hand a task off to an external party; they embed hyperspecialized third party services directly into their own operational workflows, letting their systems interact with a partner's in real time. two forces made this possible: businesses had already been digitizing and integrating their own customer facing workflows across channels domino's online ordering, which now accounts for over 85% of u.s. retail sales, automatically triggers in store cooking schedule coordination; target's app based store pickup immediately dispatches picking instructions to store associates , and once ultimately decide whether and how broadly to deploy a model, closing this gap is a management responsibility, not just a technical one. a five element "right data" framework distinguishes the problem and population of interest, the concept of "the right data" judged against six criteria — relevancy/completeness, comprehensiveness/adequate representation, freedom from bias, timeliness, clear definition, and appropriate exclusions , the actual training data used, the resulting model, and future data the model will encounter after deployment — increasingly large gaps between the right data and what's actually available at each stage signal real project risk. six penetrating questions, asked in sequence across problem definition, model development, and deployment, help managers evaluate ai developers without needing a technical background themselves: two at problem definition how and where will the model be used; how will you acquire data meeting the right data criteria , two during development what are the training data's gaps against those criteria; how will you check future data meets them , and two around deployment what controls detect future data or model drift; what are the top three ways this model could fail, and how are you mitigating them . holding back some training data as a "holdout" set to validate a model is not an acceptable substitute for genuinely evaluating future data, since holdout data is drawn from the identical source as the training data and therefore looks nothing like the real world data the model will actually encounter after deployment — amazon's facial recognition system, trained on data from one geographic area but deployed more broadly, produced exactly this "poor calibration" failure mode. concept mit sloan management review's research on data quality argues most organizations get permanently stuck in one of two dysfunctional modes rather than reaching the genuinely effective third one. in the first, unmanaged mode, data flows through a company as a "daisy chain": each department uses data to do its own job, generating new data in the process that passes to the next group in line, with people generally seeing themselves narrowly through their functional lens salesperson, vendor manager, market researcher rather than as participants in a shared data ecosystem. when someone spots an error, correcting it individually is natural but difficult and time consuming, and plenty of quality issues go undetected entirely, propagating further damage downstream as they compound. eventually, someone recognizes the cumulative business impact of this constant error stream, and the organization moves to the second mode, organized cleanup — a centralized data team implements tooling to find and fix errors faster and more cheaply. this genuinely beats pure chaos, but the gains tend to be modest: finding errors is comparatively easy, but fixing them correctly requires business context that a centralized cleanup team often lacks, trapping the organization in an endless cycle of reactive repair rather than actual improvement. the real breakthrough, per the research, comes in the third mode, proactive prevention, which requires a genuine mindset shift: in organizations that have traditionally maintained separate groups of data creators and data customers, people must come to see themselves as both simultaneously, sharing responsibility and actively collaborating — data customers clarifying and communicating their actual requirements to data creators, both sides jointly measuring data against those requirements, creators running improvement projects and implementing controls that stop errors at their source rather than downstream, and both sides continuing to evolve the arrangement together as business processes and goals change over time. making this work at scale requires a core team responsible for coordinating the overall program, training both creators and customers, maintaining shared dashboards, and keeping senior management informed — plus a category of connector roles the researchers observe recurring across organizations under titles like embedded data manager, data product manager, data ambassador, or quality champion, who sit between the core team and the working creators/customers to support the day to day work of mode 3. hellofresh's own journey through these three modes is instructive precisely because it wasn't linear or quick: the company spent longer than it should have in unmanaged mode as a fast growing startup, then moved to organized cleanup under a central engineering team that, despite genuine effort, lacked deep enough understanding of how different teams actually used the data it was cleaning — frustration mounted especially among the international marketing analytics team which needed clean data for customer sentiment analysis and personalized campaigns and the international operations business intelligence team responsible for a weekly global operating report to the c suite, and increasingly hampered by inconsistent data cascading in from hellofresh's many geographies . it was the opsbi team, out of sheer frustration, that broke through to proactive prevention first, developing a data quality framework built around formal "data contracts" data quality service level agreements that solidified its own role as a genuine data customer for the first time, while local business intelligence teams simultaneously took on genuine data creator responsibility rather than remaining purely customers themselves — with clear communication channels established between the two, quality improved quickly, though initially confined within opsbi alone. a 2020 companywide survey then made the scale of the underlying problem visible at the executive level: 61% of respondents reported unreliable data, 53% reported outright incorrect data, and nearly 84% acknowledged relying on manual workarounds to cope with these issues, findings broadly consistent with industry wide cost estimates. that survey triggered ceo level intervention, and hellofresh built a companywide data quality working group to formalize creator/customer roles and standard quality processes, launched a data literacy program to build the necessary culture, transitioned to a data mesh architecture that formalized data creators' quality responsibilities, and hired its first vice president of data to drive guidance, transparent cross team reporting, and a culture of collaboration — with embedded data product owners and data engineers subsequently added within individual business domains to sustain the improvement. the company's own account of the outcome is candid about both progress and remaining work: its self service data platform now ingests data in minutes rather than months, and quality/governance/observability are now built into that platform directly rather than bolted on afterward — but the work of decentralizing data product teams into business domains and exploring ai driven "self healing data" systems that not only observe and report on quality issues but automatically correct them remains ongoing rather than finished. the overarching lesson mit smr draws is that simply implementing better tools or assigning a dedicated team to fix data problems is not sufficient on its own — the actual breakthrough required an organizational transformation centered on the creator/customer relationship itself, with accountability for data quality ultimately residing "in the business" rather than confined to a specialist data function. how to get proactive about data quality where data quality addresses the foundational integrity of an organization's data, hbr's research on data monetization addresses the separate, downstream question of how to turn proprietary data directly into new revenue — a strategy gaining momentum as ai makes data easier to analyze, economic growth slows, and prominent examples of success accumulate amazon's advertising business built on customer interest data brought in $56 billion last year; walmart's newer online ad business, built on a similar model, now generates roughly $4 billion annually; much of linkedin's $16 billion in revenue traces directly to user data sold to recruiters; mastercard and visa have built entire advisory divisions selling transaction derived insights; reddit's stock jumped 12% on news of its 2024 data licensing deal with openai . despite this momentum, hbr's research — drawing on in depth case studies of more than 30 organizations and interviews with 12 senior executives leading monetization efforts across retail, media, tech, manufacturing, and marketing — finds most companies still struggle to choose the right approach and don't know where to begin, in part because many begin the process backward: building out technical infrastructure for a year or two before realizing they never clarified what products to build or who would actually buy them. the research's central finding is that the most successful monetization strategies start close to home, with existing partners, suppliers, and customers, for several converging reasons: existing partners already understand the specific industry and business context that makes a company's data valuable to them; the pre existing relationship makes identifying good use cases and closing deals meaningfully easier; established sales and account management relationships make it straightforward to sell a new data offering as a line item add on and scale it quickly; and staying within the existing ecosystem sidesteps privacy and data custodianship risk, since proprietary data is often bound by sharing agreements that preclude sale to data brokers or other non affiliated third parties in the first place. the alternative — selling raw, packaged data to data brokers serving hedge funds or other non strategic buyers — can look deceptively simple identify a buyer, agree a price, collect payment but tends to be genuinely riskier and to create less value than deals built on existing strategic relationships, since identifying willing buyers and negotiating fair prices with parties that have no partnership history is difficult, and such arrangements expose a company's customers and suppliers to real risk data leaks that could damage their own core business without those parties' direct involvement or consent to the arrangement. regardless of the specific path chosen, privacy, regulatory, reputational, and data security risk must be managed from day one — leading firms take care to aggregate and anonymize benchmark data before sharing it, and companies pursuing any data based offering need legal and risk management involved from the outset to assess potential problems and build mitigation plans before launch, not after a problem surfaces. none of this monetization work is possible without a genuinely solid underlying data foundation: efforts to monetize data that's poorly organized, low quality, or incomplete reliably backfire, which is precisely why the data quality discipline described above functions as a genuine prerequisite for successful monetization, not merely a nice to have. once the foundational and relationship selection questions are settled, companies face two further structural choices. the first is between direct monetization — charging customers or channel partners directly for data or data based offerings, typically structured as a subscription for a defined access period, illustrated by british retailer tesco's dunnhumby analytics division, which grew out of the company's point of sale data and eventually became its own standalone business serving retailers and consumer packaged goods companies — and indirect monetization, which embeds data into existing offerings at no additional charge, typically favored by high margin businesses for whom differentiation matters more than a direct data sales line item leading consulting firms bundling proprietary insights with their core consulting services is one pattern; sony interactive entertainment giving playstation game creators rich, free access to gameplay, development, and marketing data is another, on the logic that better informed creators build better games, which in turn drives increased platform selection and sales — sie's own analytics director noted that major industry defining innovations like fortnite have tended to emerge first within its own ecosystem as a direct result . indirect monetization, while lacking direct p&l visibility, can meaningfully increase the overall return on a company's data investment by expanding product offerings, improving operational efficiency, and strengthening customer retention — one technology provider in hbr's research found retention rates were highest specifically among customers using its data offerings, while a training and development company found providing customers with skills demand benchmarks and personalized training suggestions directly improved satisfaction and retention, and a manufacturer that shared data scorecards on service levels and inventory availability with its suppliers reduced supply chain bottlenecks and improved its own margins as a downstream effect. the second structural choice concerns how the data is actually packaged for sale, with three common approaches carrying progressively higher pricing potential and higher required investment: selling data raw, which is simplest for the seller but shifts the burden of extracting value onto the buyer best suited to buyers who lack internal data/analytics capability of their own, or whose use case doesn't fit neatly with an existing channel partner, typically selling instead to data brokers, tech companies, or other sophisticated third parties ; selling insight services, where the seller analyzes the data and prepares custom insights for the customer, both eliminating the customer's need to do that analytical work themselves and offering meaningfully more privacy and security protection, since sensitive raw details never need to leave the seller's hands mastercard advisors' aggregated, anonymized transaction network insights for banks and retailers exemplify this tier ; and selling fully commercially ready solutions — dashboards, workflows, machine learning models, and storage packaged together with the underlying insights, either as standalone products or integrated directly into an existing digital product — which command the highest prices precisely because they require the least additional work from the buyer adp's compensation benchmarking product, instacart's ad targeting platform which generated an estimated $958 million in 2024 revenue, and forddirect's dealer network analytics platform — which drove a 40% sales increase and 22% cost per lead reduction for dealers in targeted segments by combining data from dealer websites, crm systems, and back office systems into a unified customer journey view — all illustrate this highest tier . how to monetize your data forrester's research on enterprise data strategy addresses a third dimension the other two disciplines depend on: genuine cross functional coordination, examined specifically through the lens of b2c chief marketing officers, whose position illustrates both the temptation and the danger of pursuing data strategy within a single functional silo. cmos currently sit in what forrester calls a "data conundrum": four converging forces of "data deprecation" — tightening privacy laws, browser and operating system restrictions on data collection, growing consumer adoption of privacy protective tools and behaviors, and the ever taller, increasingly ubiquitous "walled gardens" maintained by platforms like amazon, facebook, and google — are significantly constraining marketers' access to the third party consumer data they've historically relied on, pushing 76% of surveyed b2c marketing executives to collect more first party data specifically in response. but forrester is explicit that simply acquiring more data doesn't automatically translate into better targeting, insight, or measurement, and identifies this belief as a common and consequential trap for several reasons: companies are frequently already drowning in customer data yet still struggle to be genuinely data driven, hampered by fragmented views of customer behavior, reactive rather than proactive privacy practices, and myopic customer journey mapping — a dynamic compounded by an industry norm, per one cvs health executive quoted, in which suggesting a brand collect less data risks being perceived as unsophisticated rather than disciplined; useful data frequently sits dormant within departmental silos, since departments tend to consider only the data they themselves own when assessing what's available to them, a mindset that produces redundant collection, limited sharing, and misinformed decisions across the wider organization a quarter of surveyed b2c marketing decision makers report organizational silos actively degrading the quality of their customer insights ; data hoarding itself constitutes a standing enterprise risk that cheap cloud storage has made easy to underestimate, since the traditional cost incentive to minimize an organization's data footprint has effectively disappeared — illustrated starkly by t mobile's 2021 breach, in which the company was found to have needlessly retained sensitive information on more than 40 million prospective and former customers most of the affected individuals weren't even current customers , resulting in a $500 million class action settlement; and data quality itself degrades measurably over time, since stale data undermines personalization and can produce a subpar customer experience even when the underlying volume of data collected looks impressive on paper. forrester's central prescription is that cmos must formalize a genuine seat at their organization's enterprise level data strategy discussions rather than pursuing a marketing specific data agenda in isolation, since a marketing only data strategy runs a high risk of further entrenching exactly the silos the organization needs to dismantle — this requires active collaboration with the cdo, cio, and finance function, and typically an "orchestra" of it, data science, risk and compliance, marketing, sales/service, and cx working together on complex cross functional use cases forrester cites pepsico's enterprise data strategy, built over seven months in direct collaboration among data scientists, data strategists, data stewards, and data engineers, as one concrete example of this kind of coordinated effort . cmos are, in forrester's framing, one of the more influential stakeholders in this cross functional effort specifically because they hold the keys to genuine customer understanding, and the research identifies four concrete responsibilities that follow from that position: surfacing and sharing business critical consumer insights that extend well beyond marketing's own use cases one global financial services firm uses marketing interaction data to anticipate credit card applications and proactively adjust onboarding processes, for instance ; turning the broader data strategy into concrete market actions that deliver measurable business value, since marketing typically owns significant volumes of customer data crm, loyalty programs, campaign data and carries substantial responsibility for actually operationalizing and scaling whatever data strategy the cdo or cto has designed — positioning marketing as a major influence on how the strategy's ultimate roi and success get measured; bridging the strategy to actual in market execution, connecting high level enterprise goals down to the people actually running marketing programs day to day, and feeding real world market response back up into the strategy's ongoing iteration; and aligning marketing's data needs and use cases with the organization's privacy policies, a responsibility forrester flags as genuinely under resourced today — with only 15% of surveyed privacy decision makers reporting that their organization's privacy team actually collaborates with marketing, despite marketing's inherently customer facing role and direct access to customer data making this collaboration gap a real and consequential risk rather than a purely theoretical one. forrester's practical guidance for cmos building a better path forward centers on tying data needs to concrete customer journey moments rather than requesting data in the abstract being specific about the business tactic a given data request supports makes it far easier for data teams to prioritize and act on, versus vague requests that get lost in an undifferentiated backlog ; genuinely assessing the risk of collecting and using customer data, including ethical and operational dimensions beyond pure security and regulatory compliance, and proactively involving legal and security teams as collaborators from the start rather than only after a conflict has already emerged; and inventorying the full range of data actually available across the enterprise, including sources well outside marketing's traditional purview call center interaction data, inventory, pricing, credit, fraud, and logistics data can all materially affect customer experience even though none of them originate within the marketing function itself , since a genuinely enterprise wide data strategy depends on marketing seeing past its own departmental data holdings to understand — and help shape — the fuller picture. the cmo’s guide to an enterprise data strategy data transformation is the ceo’s business mit smr, may 2026 supplies a single, deeply detailed case study that makes concrete what the concept's other three sources describe at the level of research findings and general prescriptions: what actual ceo level ownership of data transformation looks like in practice. when caterpillar's ceo, jim umpleby, set out in 2017 to grow services and parts revenue through digital offerings, he discovered the company's customer data was too siloed and incomplete to support that strategy — a diagnosis this concept's other sources would recognize as a mix of unmanaged mode data quality and departmental silos. rather than delegating the fix to it, umpleby's team committed three years of runway to building an enterprise data platform helios , set a public $28 billion services revenue target for 2026 to focus and measure the effort, and — the article's central structural move — made data ownership a senior business executive responsibility rather than a technology one: roughly a dozen vice presidents were recruited to own 14 enterprise data domains, evaluated monthly on their domains' data quality, while a newly created "data product owner" role echoing this concept's hellofresh case's connector roles under different titles tracked reuse and business value payoff for specific data products like the customer fleet list. the resulting platform consolidated eight legacy systems and roughly 200 dealer integration interfaces, cutting data management complexity by a factor of 30 by caterpillar's own estimate, and services revenue grew from $14 billion in 2016 to $24 billion in 2024. two governance structures — a dealer digital council giving international dealers quarterly input into the platform roadmap, and an internal demand review board ranking competing business unit project proposals against the roadmap — gave both external and internal stakeholders a genuine voice, directly preventing the re emergence of the kind of departmental data silos this concept's forrester source warns are otherwise almost inevitable. once the data foundation matured, caterpillar layered ai directly on top of it rather than launching ai as a separate initiative: machine learning models corrected data entry anomalies at ingestion, vector stores made previously unsearchable unstructured documents equipment manuals, service records available to ai systems, and an "ai digital product council" evaluated and prioritized ai use cases using the same business value discipline applied to the underlying data platform — direct evidence for this concept's broader claim that a genuine data foundation, not a parallel ai initiative, is what lets ai investments actually compound rather than stall on poor quality inputs. data transformation is the ceo’s business what managers should ask about ai models and data sets mit smr, roger w. hoerl and thomas c. redman, december 2023 applies this concept's data quality at the source discipline specifically to ai model training data, addressing a gap in how ai failures actually get diagnosed. the authors' starting observation is that most data science training focuses on the mechanics of machine learning rather than its limitations, leaving data scientists — who, per an old analytics saying, share model developers' and artists' tendency to "fall in love with their models" while data gets comparatively little attention — poorly equipped to prevent or properly diagnose ai model failures; because senior business managers ultimately decide whether and how broadly to deploy a model, closing this gap becomes a management responsibility rather than a purely technical one, even though most managers lack the technical background to spot trouble unaided. the article's central contribution is a five element "right data" framework: the problem and population of interest must be clearly and specifically defined before any data work begins echoing this concept's own emphasis on clarity of purpose before either quality or monetization work can proceed ; "the right data" is a concept, not an actual dataset — the criteria a manager hopes the data will satisfy, judged against six dimensions relevancy/completeness, comprehensiveness/adequate representation, freedom from bias, timeliness, clear definition of terms and units, and appropriate exclusions for legal, regulatory, ethical, or intellectual property reasons ; the training data actually used, which may or may not meet those criteria; the resulting trained model; and future data the model will encounter after deployment, which frequently differs from training data in ways that erode model performance over time. managers are advised to walk model developers through a sequence of six questions spanning all three project phases — at problem definition, how and where the resulting model will actually be used, and how developers plan to acquire training data meeting the right data criteria; during model development, what specific gaps exist between the training data actually obtained and those criteria, and how future data will be checked against the same standard; and around deployment, what controls will detect data or model drift over time, and what the top three failure modes are along with concrete mitigation plans for each. the article singles out one specific and common malpractice for direct criticism: validating a model using a "holdout" set carved from the same original training data the standard practice on data science competition platforms like kaggle is not an acceptable substitute for genuinely evaluating how the model performs against real future data, since holdout data is definitionally similar to training data in every way that matters — amazon's facial recognition system, trained on data drawn from one geographic area but deployed far more broadly, is offered as the canonical cautionary example of exactly the "poor calibration" failure this shortcut produces. read alongside this concept's mit smr data quality source, the right data framework extends the same proactive prevention logic — catching problems at the source rather than cleaning up after deployment — into the specific, high stakes context of ai model development, where the cost of skipping that discipline is measured in embarrassing, sometimes legally consequential, post deployment failures rather than merely degraded reporting. what managers should ask about ai models and data sets related data leadership roles evolution — the data product manager and cdo roles described there are the organizational mechanisms responsible for actually executing the quality, monetization, and cross functional strategy work described in depth in this concept ai disruption of saas business models — the monetization patterns documented here direct subscription, indirect embedding, raw/insight/product packaging tiers directly parallel the consumption based ai pricing models mckinsey documents in that concept, since both describe enterprises learning to price a previously uncommoditized asset data, then ai work for the first time gen ai organizational learning and knowledge — the "get your data and documents in order" groundwork requirement covered there for gen ai knowledge workflows is functionally the same discipline this concept's data quality section describes as a prerequisite for both ai success and data monetization ai risk prediction tool failures — documents what happens after deployment when this concept's right data due diligence questions weren't asked beforehand, across beach safety, sepsis, welfare fraud, and criminal justice ai risk prediction tools open questions neither the data quality nor the data monetization source addresses how an organization should sequence the two disciplines when both are underdeveloped simultaneously — whether reaching "proactive prevention" mode is a hard prerequisite before attempting data monetization, or whether some monetization work e.g., selling raw data to sophisticated buyers who will clean it themselves can proceed in parallel with an unfinished internal quality transformation. the cmo's guide source is from forrester 2023 and predates the more recent ai driven data strategy pieces elsewhere in the vault — it's unclear how the four "data deprecation" forces it describes privacy laws, browser restrictions, consumer privacy tool adoption, walled gardens interact with the more recent ai driven data monetization opportunities described in "how to monetize your data," since ai training data licensing deals like reddit's with openai represent a use case for consumer data that the cmo's guide doesn't address at all. the right data source doesn't address how its six question framework should be adapted for gen ai/llm projects specifically, where "training data" often means a vast, largely uncurated internet scale corpus rather than the bounded, purpose collected datasets its credit scoring and facial recognition examples assume. sources how to get proactive about data quality — mit smr's three mode data quality framework and hellofresh's multiyear journey through it. how to monetize your data — hbr's 30 organization research on direct/indirect data monetization strategy and packaging tiers. the cmo’s guide to an enterprise data strategy — forrester's research on why cmos must pursue enterprise level, cross functional data strategy rather than a marketing only agenda. data transformation is the ceo’s business — mit smr, barbara wixom, 2026 05 21; caterpillar's helios data platform case study in ceo led, business owned not it owned data transformation, extending directly into ai. what managers should ask about ai enterprise-negotiation-tactics: summary how skilled negotiators create leverage even without a clear batna — through partial alternatives, procedural moves, and reframing threats as warnings. also covers why large company negotiations structurally underperform due to agency and alignment problems, and how replacing deal review boards with proactive "deal value boards" fixes both. highlights when a complete alternative to a deal doesn't exist, partial alternatives that only cover a fraction of the need can still shift negotiating dynamics: a tech company facing an intransigent sole electronics supplier found two smaller suppliers that together covered just 30% of its volume, and used that partial coverage to force better pricing from the incumbent rather than accepting an unaffordable increase. negotiating when there is no plan b dependence between negotiating parties is usually more balanced than it feels: a company that relies heavily on a sole source supplier is often just as important to that supplier's revenue and fixed cost coverage, meaning even a party that seems to have "no alternative" often retains real leverage — genuine walk away brinkmanship is rare the authors saw it only once in 25 years of dealmaking . negotiating when there is no plan b beyond a formal batna, negotiators can pursue "procedural alternatives" — unilateral actions that don't require the other side's agreement, such as paying invoices based on the lowest price a supplier charges anywhere globally with a note explaining the "correction" rather than formally demanding renegotiation, using inertia and tacit rather than active consent to shift the relationship without a confrontation. negotiating when there is no plan b reframing a walk away possibility as a warning "we can't afford this, so we'll be forced to find someone else" rather than a threat "agree or we cut you off" avoids the coercion counterthreat spiral, since warnings signal self protection rather than an intent to harm the other side — and appealing to fairness "why are you demanding this?" can extract concessions that raw power plays cannot, since people will sometimes concede rather than be shown to be acting unfairly. negotiating when there is no plan b enterprise negotiations underperform not from negotiator skill gaps but from two structural problems: the agency problem frontline negotiators are incentivized toward closing any deal — commission, time pressure — rather than the enterprise's actual interests, so organizations restrict their authority, turning them into "couriers" who must repeatedly seek approval and the alignment problem in complex, multi stakeholder deals, forcing early pre negotiation consensus on the most conservative acceptable terms leaves negotiators no room to explore creative trade offs . why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals the counterintuitive fix for the agency problem is to give negotiators no commitment authority at all, reframing them as problem solvers who explore options and bring a recommended business plan back to decision makers, rather than agents defending preapproved minimums — removing the incentive to make self interested concessions just to close, while letting them engage counterparties creatively without triggering internal vetoes. why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals organizations should first decide which deals and issues are actually worth negotiating hard, since most contract terms can be resolved at reasonable "market standard" levels without real loss of value — the operative question is not how large an issue is but how much of that value is genuinely at stake in negotiating it versus accepting a market norm, and companies increasingly use generative ai agents to close standardized, low variance deals automatically. why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals traditional deal review boards drbs , which evolved from capital project approval processes, should be reimagined as proactive "deal value boards" dvbs that give negotiating teams an enterprise wide view of related deals and current/future leverage, and that broker internal "side deals" compensating business units that would otherwise block a proposal that benefits the company overall — evolving from expectation setting early in a deal, to problem solving support during negotiation, to a final go/no go decision made by a small group once options are fully understood. why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals concept two complementary pieces of negotiation research address the same underlying challenge — how organizations extract more value from high stakes deals — from opposite ends: one focuses on individual negotiator tactics when a walk away alternative seems unavailable, the other on the organizational structures that prevent even skilled negotiators from creating value at scale. on the individual tactics side, the starting premise is that the absence of a clear batna best alternative to a negotiated agreement, the term roger fisher and william ury introduced in getting to yes doesn't actually mean a negotiator is powerless — it usually means they haven't expanded their search enough. the first lever is the power of partial alternatives: when negotiators search for a batna, they typically look for one complete substitute that addresses every problem, but a breakthrough often comes instead from an option that only partially replaces the deal on the table. a high tech company entirely dependent on one supplier for critical electronic components, facing repeated price increases and degrading service, identified two smaller, qualified suppliers that together could cover only 30 percent of its total volume — but that partial coverage was enough to credibly reduce its dependence on the incumbent and extract better pricing in exchange for a modest volume commitment, rather than accepting an unaffordable increase under the illusion that its only alternative was catastrophic supply disruption. negotiating when there is no plan b a second lever is recognizing that dependence between negotiating parties is almost always more balanced than it feels from inside the weaker seeming position: if a company relies heavily on a sole source supplier, that supplier typically also depends heavily on the company's revenue, and the higher the switching costs for the customer, the more painful losing that customer usually is for the supplier too — meaning genuine walk away brinkmanship is exceedingly rare in practice the authors, who have advised on hundreds of negotiations across three decades, saw a deal actually blow up under firm but reasonable pressure only once . a global manufacturer facing a coatings supplier demanding a 10 percent price increase during contract renewal discovered that, although its business represented "only" 10 percent of the supplier's revenue, that revenue came from one of the supplier's most profitable and specialized product lines, meaning losing it would force costly retooling and strain the supplier's cash flow far more than the raw percentage suggested — illustrating that even a seemingly weak negotiating position can rest on hidden supplier vulnerabilities worth actively researching rather than assuming away. a third lever, for situations where a genuine batna search keeps coming up empty, is pursuing procedural alternatives: unilateral actions a negotiator can take without needing the other side's formal agreement, distinguishing between active consent an explicit "yes" and tacit consent proceeding as long as the counterpart doesn't actively object . a global microprocessor company discovered a supplier was charging wildly inconsistent prices for identical components shipped to different sites; rather than opening a formal negotiation it couldn't easily win given it had no qualified alternative supplier , it simply began paying every invoice at the lowest price the supplier charged anywhere, with a note explaining the "correction" — and continued receiving shipments uninterrupted for nearly a year, saving significant money each month, until the supplier finally escalated in a notably non aggressive tone once market conditions had shifted back toward better balance. related to this is the principal agent distinction: negotiators facing a large counterparty organization should distinguish the company from the specific individuals at the table, since a client's business may be small relative to the counterparty's total revenue but critical to a specific negotiating unit's targets or a specific negotiator's personal quota — leverage that headline revenue comparisons obscure entirely. finally, communicating a walk away possibility is a delicate art: framing it as a threat "agree or we cut off shipments" triggers a coercive, defensive spiral, while framing the identical substance as a warning "we can't afford this, so we'll be forced to look elsewhere" signals self protection rather than an intent to harm, which is far less likely to provoke a counterthreat — and when power plays alone don't move a counterparty, appealing to fairness "why are you demanding this?" can succeed where raw leverage cannot, since people sometimes concede simply because they can't justify their position once asked to explain it. negotiating when there is no plan b the second, complementary piece of research addresses why large organizations underperform at negotiation systematically, even when individual negotiators are skilled. two structural problems drive this: the agency problem, where negotiators act on the organization's behalf but their personal incentives commission on closing a sale, time pressure to move on to the next of dozens of supplier relationships don't perfectly match the enterprise's actual interests, leading organizations to restrict negotiator authority so tightly that dealmakers become, in effect, couriers who must repeatedly return to superiors for approval on every concession — a dynamic that slows deals, damages credibility, and strips away the room to solve problems creatively at the table. and the alignment problem, which compounds as deals grow more complex: in multiproduct, multiregion, or cross functional negotiations, each internal stakeholder sales wants pricing and revenue, engineering wants realistic deadlines, legal wants minimized risk needs to be satisfied, and forcing early pre negotiation consensus typically means agreeing on the most conservative minimums acceptable to everyone — after which negotiators have essentially no room left to explore genuine trade offs, and if a counterparty won't accept those preapproved terms, the negotiator must reopen the internal debate from scratch, repeatedly, prolonging the process and eroding trust on both sides of the table. common organizational fixes often make this worse rather than better: "guardrails" that preapprove specific concessions in advance tend to grow so long and restrictive that they almost never match the realities of a live negotiation one lead negotiator described winning a deal within tight guardrails as something that "never happens" , and traditional deal review boards drbs — which evolved out of capital project approval, where a project can be approved or rejected on the basis of projected risk and return alone — simply replicate the authority parceling problem with more senior people involved, since a negotiation additionally requires guesswork about what an external counterparty will actually accept. why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals the prescribed fix works by attacking both problems simultaneously rather than separately. first, organizations should decide upfront which deals and issues are genuinely worth a full negotiation effort at all — not every deal merits it, and within any single complex deal, not every issue does either. the operative test isn't how large an issue is in absolute terms but how much of that value is actually at stake in negotiating it versus simply accepting a reasonable, market standard term: in mature markets like eurobonds, most terms already proceed on standardized forms with only a small number of genuinely negotiated adjustments, and companies increasingly use generative ai agents to close standardized, low variance deals automatically within set parameters, freeing skilled human negotiators for the comparatively few issues where negotiation can genuinely change the outcome. second, and most counterintuitively, the fix for the agency problem is not giving negotiators more authority but giving them essentially none: reframing them as problem solvers tasked with exploring the counterparty's actual needs and constraints and bringing back a recommended business plan, rather than agents empowered to make binding commitments within a narrow, preapproved band. removing commitment authority removes the incentive to make self interested concessions purely to close a deal directly addressing agency , and because the negotiator's job becomes exploration rather than defending fixed minimums, they can engage in genuinely creative problem solving with a counterparty without triggering internal vetoes at every turn addressing alignment . a midsize technology company renewing a critical $180 million partnership deal used exactly this approach — requesting authority to explore innovative structures with the incumbent partner and to open unauthorized, no commitment talks with a disliked rival, which the board initially resisted but ultimately allowed; the rival partner turned out to be a genuinely viable option, and the resulting leverage helped the company close nearly $1 billion in improved terms with its original incumbent partner. third, this requires replacing early, locked in stakeholder sign off with ongoing, two way consultation throughout the negotiation — testing volume and delivery trade offs with business unit leaders, payment term trade offs with finance, service capacity trade offs with operations, as new information emerges from the actual talks — rather than freezing every internal position before external negotiation even begins, since forcing people to commit early to minimum acceptable terms predictably leads them to inflate those minimums defensively, hiding the organization's true fallback position even from its own negotiators. finally, the traditional drb should evolve into a "deal value board" dvb : a proactive, cross silo body whose job is not merely to approve deals but to give negotiators visibility into related deals and future opportunities elsewhere in the organization that could strengthen current leverage, and to broker internal "side deals" that compensate business units who would otherwise block a proposal that benefits the enterprise as a whole — evolving from managing stakeholder expectations early in a deal's life, to active problem solving support as talks progress, to a final, well informed go/no go decision made by a small group only once every viable option has actually been surfaced and understood. why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals related algorithmic auditing frameworks — the stakeholder mapping discipline of the ethical matrix parallels this concept's principal agent distinction between a counterparty organization and the specific individuals negotiating on its behalf pyramid principle — minto's structured approach to organizing an argument is a complementary communication discipline for the "business plan" recommendations this concept's empowered but uncommitted negotiators bring back to decision makers open questions neither source addresses how the "no commitment authority" negotiator model should handle genuinely time critical negotiations, where the delay inherent in bringing recommendations back to decision makers could itself cost the deal. sources negotiating when there is no plan b — hbr's tactics for creating negotiating leverage without a clear batna: partial alternatives, procedural moves, warnings versus threats, and fairness appeals. why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals — danny ertel hbr on the agency and alignment problems in enterprise negotiation, and the shift from deal review boards to deal value boards.
executive-ai-digital-twins: summary a small but growing number of executives are creating ai replicas trained on their own writing, speeches, and communication style to handle routine tasks, public appearances, and employee questions on their behalf. early adopters report substantial time savings, but the practice raises unresolved questions about accuracy, workforce acceptance, and who owns the accumulated knowledge. highlights an executive ai digital twin is built by training a system on an individual's own emails, speeches, podcasts, articles, and interviews so it can answer questions, draft communications, or appear at events in that person's communication style. linkedin co founder reid hoffman's "reid ai," trained on 22 years of his own material, has delivered more than 75 addresses and presentations since its 2024 launch, speaks 74 languages, and saves hoffman an estimated 50% of his time in weeks it's deployed. digital twins are being used for internal coaching and mentorship, not just external appearances: greif's "balabot" has interacted with nearly 3,300 employees since december, and quantium health's "virtual brian" helped one executive manager recognize she had underrated her own accomplishments in a self evaluation. a december report from the institute for corporate productivity concluded digital work twins could become the most significant productivity multiplier since the personal computer, with reid hoffman predicting most companies over 50 employees will have executive ai twins within a decade, and rank and file employee twins following within two. digital twins have real failure modes requiring human oversight: hallucination reid ai has invented answers to opinion questions , tonal misfires failing to sound appropriately serious or light , and outright technical glitches one executive's twin visibly malfunctioned, repeating the same line, in front of a live conference audience . employee acceptance is not automatic — early resistance is common staff at one firm objected to having their emails used to train a twin but is often resolved through opt out mechanisms for sensitive personal or work content and scoped access to only explicitly authorized material. ownership of a digital twin's accumulated knowledge when an employee departs is an unresolved legal and organizational question; one company's policy lets a departing employee take their twin's likeness and personal expertise while the employer retains proprietary business knowledge the twin accumulated. the clearest governance principle articulated so far is that digital twins should support human decision making rather than substitute for human accountability, particularly in supervisory or legal adjacent contexts where a misstatement could create real liability. concept too much work to do? have your digital twin handle it wsj, may 2026 documents an emerging executive practice: creating an ai driven replica of oneself, trained on one's own writing, speeches, and communication patterns, to absorb routine work that would otherwise consume an executive's time directly. reid hoffman's "reid ai" is the most developed example — trained on 22 years of his books, speeches, podcasts, and articles, it has delivered more than 75 addresses and presentations since 2024 with human preparation involved , speaks 74 languages, and by hoffman's own estimate saves him roughly half his time in the weeks it is deployed. other examples extend the pattern to internal, one on one coaching contexts rather than only public facing appearances: greif's chief human resources officer built "balabot," which has interacted with nearly 3,300 employees seeking guidance since its december launch, while quantium health ceo brian hartzer's "virtual brian" has been used by direct reports to prepare for performance reviews, in one case helping an executive manager recognize she had underrated her own contributions in a self assessment. adoption is not without friction. advocates frame the trend in ambitious terms — a december report from the institute for corporate productivity's chief strategy officer concludes digital work twins could be "the most significant productivity multiplier since the personal computer," and hoffman predicts within a decade most companies with more than 50 employees will assign trained virtual counterparts to senior roles, with rank and file employee twins following within a similar timeframe. but the article documents concrete, present day failure modes: reid ai has hallucinated answers to simple opinion questions and occasionally misjudges tone failing to look serious after a joke , while one executive's public facing digital twin visibly malfunctioned mid event, stuttering and repeating the same line in front of roughly 200 conference attendees, prompting the executive to shut it down live and acknowledge "ai isn't ready for the main stage." workforce acceptance is also not automatic: employees at one firm initially resisted having their own emails and work documents used to train a colleague's digital twin, a concern addressed through explicit opt out provisions for sensitive personal or work content. a senior intellectual property counsel quoted in the piece frames the emerging governance principle as one where digital twins with any supervisory role must "support human decision making, not replace legal review or human accountability" — reflecting the real risk that an ai double could misstate employment policy or other legally consequential information without a human catching the error. the article closes on the practice's most unresolved dimension: ownership of the accumulated knowledge inside a digital twin once the underlying employee leaves the company. algorithm to the data rather than the data to the algorithm. a four type data framework poor, horizontal, vertical, rich tells business leaders which kind of external partner to seek to improve their own ai systems. highlights federated learning, combined with specialized encryption, lets an ai model or algorithm be trained using data from multiple decentralized servers controlled by different organizations while preserving the privacy of the individuals or organizations whose data is used — in effect, sending the algorithm to the data rather than sending the data to the algorithm. zurich insurance group used a commercial federated learning platform to improve a predictive algorithm with data from telecom company orange, without orange ever releasing any data — the collaboration foundation-models: summary stanford's 2021 report that coined the term "foundation model" for ai systems bert, gpt 3, clip trained on broad data at scale and adaptable to a wide range of downstream tasks. covers the emergent capabilities and homogenization risk this scale produces, and the report's domain by domain analysis of opportunity healthcare, law, education, robotics and risk. highlights the report identifies a paradigm shift in ai driven by models like bert, dall e, and gpt 3 that are trained on broad data at scale and adaptable to a wide range of downstream tasks, coining the term "foundation model" specifically to underscore that these models are critically central to modern ai applications yet remain incomplete on their own — a base that must be adapted, not a finished product. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models a foundation model is defined precisely as any model trained on broad data generally via self supervision at scale that can be adapted, such as through fine tuning, to a wide range of downstream tasks; bert, gpt 3, and clip are given as the paradigm examples circa 2021. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models though foundation models rest on standard deep learning and transfer learning techniques, their sheer scale produces genuinely new emergent capabilities not present in smaller models, and their broad effectiveness across many tasks creates a strong incentive toward homogenization — using the same underlying model as the base for many different applications — which is powerful leverage but also means any defect in the foundation model gets inherited by every model built on top of it. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models despite the accelerating pace of deployment, the report stresses that there remains no clear understanding of how foundation models actually work, when they fail, or the true extent of what they're capable of, precisely because their most significant capabilities emerge unpredictably from scale rather than from any single traceable design decision. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models gpt 3's scale illustrates just how far this had already stretched expectations by 2021: 175 billion parameters, adaptable via natural language prompts alone to perform passably on a wide range of tasks it was never explicitly trained to do. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models the report organizes foundation model capabilities into five areas that power downstream applications: processing different modalities language, vision , affecting the physical world robotics , and performing reasoning and interaction with humans — each requiring distinct technical innovation, since a model's raw capability doesn't automatically transfer into being useful for a specific application domain. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models robotics faces a structurally different challenge from language and vision: because it's anchored to the physical world rather than benefiting from abundant raw data and cheap virtual application environments, developing foundation models for robotics specifically requires finding sufficient data of the right form — the report points to generic, environment agnostic video of humans as one promising source that could help bridge this data gap. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models applied to healthcare and biomedicine, foundation models are well suited to domains where expert knowledge is scarce and expensive, since abundant multimodal data images, text, molecular data already exists and improved sample efficiency in adaptation directly reduces the cost of expert time; applied to law, ample data exists in legal documents and generative capability suits many of law's core tasks, but significant improvement is still needed before models can reliably reason across sources to produce genuinely truthful long form legal documents; applied to education, the report sees clear potential for adaptive, personalized learning given foundation models' sample efficient adaptation and open ended generative and interactive capabilities, provided models improve at reasoning about student cognition and aligning with actual learning goals. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models concept stanford's center for research on foundation models introduced the term "foundation model" in this 2021 report to describe a paradigm shift already underway in ai: models such as bert, dall e, and gpt 3, trained on broad data at scale typically via self supervision and adaptable — through techniques like fine tuning — to a wide range of downstream tasks, rather than built and trained for one narrow purpose. the term is deliberately chosen to capture a duality: these models are critically central to the modern ai applications built on top of them, yet remain incomplete on their own, since a foundation model requires further adaptation before it becomes any specific, useful application. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models the report's central technical observation is that foundation models, while built from standard deep learning and transfer learning techniques that predate them, exhibit genuinely emergent capabilities once trained at sufficient scale — capabilities not present in smaller versions of the same architecture and not straightforwardly predictable from the training process itself. gpt 3, with 175 billion parameters, illustrates how far this had already stretched expectations: it can be adapted via natural language prompts alone to perform passably on tasks it was never explicitly trained to do. this same scale driven effectiveness across many different tasks creates a powerful incentive toward homogenization — building many different downstream applications on top of the same underlying foundation model rather than training bespoke models for each — which the report frames as a double edged development: homogenization provides real leverage one well built foundation model can power many applications efficiently but also means that any defect, bias, or failure mode inherited by the foundation model propagates automatically into every application built on top of it. compounding this risk, the report is explicit that despite the accelerating pace of real world deployment, there is currently no clear understanding of how these models actually work internally, when or why they fail, or the true boundaries of what they're capable of — a genuine knowledge gap, not merely a communication problem, precisely because the most significant capabilities emerge unpredictably from scale rather than from any single traceable design choice researchers can point to. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models the report organizes the capabilities that power foundation model applications into several areas: processing different modalities language and vision being the most mature , affecting the physical world through robotics, performing reasoning, and interacting with humans — treating each as requiring its own distinct technical innovation, since raw model capability doesn't automatically translate into usefulness for any specific application domain. language and vision have led the way, in the report's account, precisely because they benefit from abundant raw training data and cheap, virtual application environments in which to test and deploy models; robotics faces a structurally harder path because it remains anchored to the physical world, lacking both the abundance of easily gathered data and the low cost virtual testbeds available to language and vision — the report points to generic, environment agnostic video footage of humans performing tasks as one promising, non domain specific data source that could help close this gap for robotics foundation models specifically. applied across specific domains, the report finds foundation models particularly well suited to healthcare and biomedical research, where expert knowledge is scarce and costly, since abundant multimodal data already exists images, text, molecular structures and the sample efficiency foundation models bring to adaptation directly reduces the amount of expensive expert time required; to legal applications, where ample data already exists in the form of legal documents and generative capability suits many of the field's core writing tasks, though the report cautions that significant further improvement is needed before models can reliably reason across multiple sources to produce genuinely truthful, coherent long form legal documents rather than merely plausible sounding ones; and to education, where the report sees clear potential for adaptive, personalized learning applications — given foundation models' open ended generative capabilities such as automatically generating practice problems and interactive capabilities such as giving feedback to teachers — contingent on models improving at reasoning about student cognition and aligning generated content with actual learning goals rather than superficially plausible content. across all of these domains, the report's overarching argument is that foundation model research, at the time of writing still largely confined to computer science and concentrated in the tech industry, has clear potential to extend ai's reach into many sectors well beyond tech — meaning the effects both beneficial and harmful of homogenization, emergent capability, and incomplete understanding are set to become more pervasive across people's lives, not less, as adoption spreads. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models related ai ml fundamentals — the core
